author: Mada Masr
title: Lina Attalah in custody after court issues LE3 mn fine, orders Mada Masr’s closure
content:
Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah was fined LE3 million by the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, which convicted her on charges of managing an unlicensed website, issuing an order for the website’s closure. Attalah was taken into custody after the issue of the ruling.


Tuesday’s session at the ninth circuit of the New Cairo Misdemeanor Court, presided over by judge Mohamed Mubarak, was temporarily suspended for deliberations after Attalah’s defense counsel requested time to review the case file.


After the court returned from deliberations, the judge ordered the courtroom cleared of everyone except Attalah and her defense counsel, the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights’ executive director Hossam Bahgat, who was also present, told Mada Masr. The room then filled with plainclothes officers and guards, with a National Security Agency officer in attendance, he added.


The presiding judge and a Supreme State Security Prosecution representative returned to the session and the judge announced that the court has decided to stand by its rejection of all the procedural arguments presented by the defense, including requests to bring in any documentation or hear any witnesses.


The judge then asked the defense team to present its plea. The counsel insisted that it would not submit a plea as long as its requests were unanswered by the court.


The judge then abruptly asked for a lawyer unknown to any member of the defense counsel to be brought in, “in a move that astonished all those present,” said Bahgat, and announced that the court decided to appoint a lawyer for Attalah.


At that point, all members of the defense counsel cried out to reject the court’s appointment of a lawyer when the eight chosen lawyers were present. Attalah herself spoke to say she did not accept the court-appointed lawyer acting on her behalf, an objection the judge refused to have recorded in the session’s minutes.


“In an even more shocking move,” said Bahgat, the judge himself began to log down the requests of the court-appointed lawyer, without the lawyer having said a word. The judge then read out the conviction amid shouts and protests from the defense counsel.


The judge sentenced Attalah to the maximum possible penalty: a LE3 million fine, the closure of Mada Masr’s website and the confiscation of its property.


Security personnel then surrounded Attalah, lifted her off the ground and took her out of the courtroom, where she remains in custody in the courthouse.

author: Carmen Esselink
title: Cape Verde’s Elections Were Loud. Its Voters Are Increasingly Silent
content:
On the 29th of October, before 10 o’clock in the morning, a car with speakers has already driven twice through my neighbourhood in Mindelo, the city of Cesária Évora and of Cape Verde’s best-known Carnival, blasting MpD (

Movimento para a Democracia,

Movement for Democracy) viewpoints and a jingle. I notice I’m immediately annoyed, because I’m trying to conduct an interview from home and the noise keeps interrupting the conversation. The same car passes twice more that day. Three days later, on Sunday 1 November, a whole procession of floats drives along the beach, honking, accompanied by Cape Verdean and PAICV (

Partido Africano da Independência de Cabo Verde

, African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde) flags, candidate headshots and more jingles, while my boyfriend and I are trying to get onto the road in the car. Election season in Cape Verde has begun: a very loud time, and a disruptive one. As an outsider, I wonder whether it has the desired effect, people voting for a certain party, or the opposite: abstention.


The noise is meant to bring people to the polls. In May’s parliamentary election, most of them stayed home. Just

46.5 percent of the 416,096 registered voters

 cast a ballot, down from 57.4 percent in 2021 and 66 percent in 2016. Yet Cape Verde is often held up as one of Africa’s most stable democracies, and in May the PAICV, which grew out of the independence movement, returned to power after ten years in opposition. It was the loudest election I’ve ever witnessed, with central roads closed for concerts and rallies, pickups with speakers crawling through town, and people handing out partisan t-shirts. Six months later, the country was campaigning again, this time for the presidential election on 15 November.


A concert stage goes up on Rua Lisboa in Mindelo ahead of the parliamentary elections of May 2026. Photo: Carmen Esselink


On 12 November at 8pm, the band

Corda do Sol

 plays on Rua Lisboa, ahead of a speech by President José Maria Neves, backed by the PAICV. At the same time, Joana Rosa, the MpD’s candidate and former justice minister, is holding a concert with the band Pendrive in Monte Sossego, another neighbourhood. While I’m standing in the crowd, I hear people behind me say: ‘Come on, the concert’s almost over and the speech starts after this. Let’s go to the other concert now.’ With street vendors with drinks and food around the corner as part of the rival political campaigns, it’s a night out for many people: they run into acquaintances and catch up over the music.


There are two kinds of people in the crowd. Some wear party t-shirts and make it very clear who they’re here for and who they’ll vote for. The others come for the music and would rather not talk about their political preference. They tell me they’re afraid of repercussions. ‘If I say I’m voting for this one and the other party gets wind of it, I’m afraid they’ll obstruct me in other matters,’ one person says. That fear isn’t unusual: in

a 2024 Afrobarometer survey

, more than one in five Cape Verdeans said it was likely that powerful people could find out how they voted, despite the secret ballot. A few people at the concert tell me they won’t vote. Others are still undecided, but say it matters to them to use their vote. A few more say they’ll cast a blank ballot.


The band Corda do Sol plays on Rua Lisboa in Mindelo ahead of a speech by President José Maria Neves, 12 November 2026. Photo: Carmen Esselink


When I asked António Tavares to describe election season, he started much further back, before independence. A choreographer, dancer and researcher, Tavares is the artistic director of the Mindelo Cultural Centre and a co-founder of Bombu Mininu, a cultural space in São Vicente. He was a child when Cape Verde gained independence in 1975, and he says he has never belonged to a political party. According to Tavares, music once carried the dream of independence. Musicians, poets and thinkers imagined the country through lyrics before it existed. ‘Music is the material,’ he says. ’It’s our way of communicating. We are a sonic entity. Why music? Because we knew we were going to leave here. If we had to leave, we had to come up with a Morse code.’


To this day, music is one of the main ways Cape Verdeans communicate. Cape Verde’s historic World Cup debut this year came with its own anthem,

Nôs Óra Dja Txiga

, bringing together artists from across the islands. While the World Cup gave Cape Verdeans a song …

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: ‘I did fear for my life,’ RCMP officer testifies at inquest into shooting death of Rankin Inlet man
content:
In a tense second day at the coroner’s inquest into the death of a 21-year-old Rankin Inlet man, an officer who fired at the victim said that he feared for his safety.


Const. Clark Plaetinck was part of the RCMP’s emergency response team that flew in from Winnipeg on Nov. 6, 2021, while Trey Angootealuk was in a standoff with police. Plaetinck testified that after chemical irritants were deployed through the back window of the truck Angootealuk was in, the man exited with his rifle appearing to be turned toward them.


“I feared for my safety at that point, so I used my firearm to stop him,” Plaetinck told the inquest jury Tuesday in Rankin Inlet.


On Nov. 6, 2021, Angootealuk hijacked a truck, drove it to the outskirts of town, shot at police officers, then began a standoff with police that lasted several hours. Police fatally shot him early the following morning.


The inquest by Nunavut Chief Coroner Marianna Cervantes will determine the circumstances surrounding Angootealuk’s death. It began Monday at the Siniktarvik Hotel in Rankin Inlet and is scheduled to last until Friday. The coroner’s office gave Nunatsiaq News a video link to cover the inquest remotely.


Nikolai Sittman, the Angootealuk family’s lawyer, asked why officers didn’t shoot him somewhere non-fatal.


Plaetnick said they didn’t want to risk missing him because they were shooting from afar.


At one point, during a pause in Plaetnick’s testimony, an audience member could be heard yelling a profanity at him.


Sgt. Russ Hulme, another member of the RCMP’s emergency response team, also testified Tuesday.


He said he flew to Rankin Inlet from Winnipeg the night the standoff began.


Hulme and one other team member launched a gas canister into the stolen truck from its rear window, right before Angootealuk’s death.


Drone footage of that moment was played at the inquest.


It showed Angootealuk exiting the vehicle. Soon after police had shot at him, he laid on the ground outside the driver’s door.


After the footage played, some inquest attendees could be heard crying. Some left the room.


Jury members asked Hulme why his team, which consisted of four members, didn’t consider shooting at the man’s vehicle to immobilize it.


Doing so would not have separated Angootealuk from his gun, and any escalation on their end may have risked a violent reaction from him, Hulme said.


“It sounds like it’s an easy task, but it carries risks,” he said.


Earlier on Tuesday, Sgt. Benjamin Comely, the detachment commander at the time, also testified.

 


Comely said Angootealuk had a tactical advantage at one point during the standoff because of where he was positioned.


“I did fear for my life,” Comely said.

 


Coroner’s inquests are mandatory under Nunavut law for all deaths involving an on-duty police officer. They do not determine the guilt or innocence of anyone involved.


It will resume Tuesday at 9:30 a.m. CT, with more RCMP personnel expected to testify.

author: Dennis Ward
title: Métis country singer Catie St. Germain and her journey from insecurity to the top of the charts
content:
It has only been about three years since

Catie St. Germain

 released his first single but she has been racking up the accolades, ever since.


Growing up, St. Germain says she had a front-row seat to a legendary musician and television host, crushing it on stage every night.


Her grandfather, Ray St. Germain, is a Canadian Country Music Hall of Fame inductee, who also created and hosted a nationally syndicated variety show,

Big Sky Country.


However, having a famous grandfather and a very musical family did not ensure she would follow in their footsteps.


St. Germain’s mother even tried to push her in another direction.


“She didn’t have the best experience, I think doing music. The pressure of it all was a lot for her, so, she kind of steered us away. She didn’t want her kids to have to go through the hardships of the music industry and everything,” says St. Germain on the latest episode of

Face to Face.


“For a long time I just didn’t think this was something in the cards for me. But I did perform, I did sing. I joined a rock tribute band and was kind of touring with them for a while but I ended up quitting and just having kids myself and thinking it was easier and better to do the 9 to 5 thing and obviously the scheduling worked better for having kids. And then I got back to it though.


“I really wasn’t fulfilled and so I decided to write my original song,

The Taxman

 in 2023 and release that and see what would come of it and it just sparked a whole new passion for me,” adds St. Germain.


The time on the road had St. Germain feeling like she was away from her family all of the time.


Breaking out on her own was also a way to challenge herself and show some bravery.


“I’ve always been somebody who is a little bit more insecure and never would try, I didn’t want to put myself out there. Even in the family too, I would do the family shows with them but I was always the shy one, like I wasn’t the one that was out there, at all. Very shy, very timid. I had my kids and I just really wanted to show them that they could do anything they put their mind to and they can be brave and if I was going to tell them to do that, then I probably should do it too,” says St. Germain.


The reaction to that first song and following EP,

Cleaning House (Or Trying)

 was even more incredible that St. Germain had imagined.


St. Germain and Don Amero perform their duet Home on Face to Face. Photo: Dennis Ward/APTN.


In the three years since then, St. Germain has sang the national anthem at the 2025 CFL Grey Cup in Winnipeg, been named one of Amazon Music’s breakthrough artists, and racked up three number one hits on the Indigenous Music Countdown.


In November at the 2026 Manitoba Country Music Awards, St. Germain was named Female Artist of the Year and took home Interactive Artist, Duo or Group of the Year, for the third straight year.


St. Germain says social media has allowed her to reach a bigger audience.


“I think too, a lot of people get to relate to me as a human, as a person and not just the music, which is really fun. Again, I just create better relationships that way and I think it entices them more to go listen to the music after that,” says St. Germain.


St. Germain’s latest single, a duet with Don Amero called

Home

hit the Indigenous Music Countdown on November 21.


Her next single

, I Ain’t Free

will be released on Nov. 27.

Métis country singer Catie St. Germain and her journey from insecurity to the top of the charts

APTN News

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Poll: Most Dems Want Congress to Defund War Next Month, Even at Risk of Shutdown
content:
Top Republicans have signaled an openness to defunding the war, as Democrats like Hakeem Jeffries have demurred.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

New polling finds that the majority of Democrats want members of Congress to use next month’s government funding bill to withhold funds for the Iran war, a strategy embraced by progressives and figures like Senate majority leader candidate Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) to end the war as soon as possible.

According to University of Maryland polling conducted this past weekend, 51 percent of Democrats say that they support the use of the upcoming funding bill, with a deadline of December 11, to defund the war even if it risks a government shutdown or a presidential veto. By contrast, only 16 percent of Democrats said they oppose the idea — a -35 point margin — while 32 percent said they don’t know.

The idea is also narrowly favored when responses from all ideologies are considered, 31 percent support to 28 percent opposition, despite 48 percent of Republicans opposing the idea.

Earlier this month, a group of four senators — Van Hollen, Michael Bennet (D-Colorado), Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), and Tammy Duckworth (D-Illinois) — vowed in a joint statement to oppose any funding bill that would fund the war. Lawmakers in favor of the effort have made clear that their intention is to effectively dare President Donald Trump to shut down the government in order to fund his war.

“Congress cannot allow Trump to continue his conflict — we must force him to end it,” the lawmakers said. “When we vote on appropriations, we intend to fund the government and stop funds for this war.”

The proposal is imminently achievable. The Washington Post reported this week that top Republicans have said that they are open to allowing the bill to be used to cut off funding for the war in exchange for keeping the government funded. The Post cited Senate Appropriations Committee Chair Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-South Dakota) as two Republicans who said they are open to the effort.

Thune said that he is “open to anything that keeps the government funded and makes sure that we’ve got our military and national security requirements and needs met.”

In other words, the Democratic base wants Congress to defund the war at the soonest possible opportunity; several Democrats in Congress are pushing for the proposal; and even Republican leaders may be on board.

Part of the reason for this broad-based support may be the vast unpopularity of the war, in which U.S.-Israeli strikes have killed roughly 3,500 people in Iran.

University of Maryland’s polling found that a staggering 80 percent of Democrats say that they want the war to end now “regardless of the terms,” meaning that they would be fine with accepting any of Iran’s and U.S.’s terms in exchange for the war’s end. A majority of all respondents felt the same, at 55 percent, compared to 21 percent who said they prefer the current course, and 18 percent saying they favor a military escalation.

Experts have said that defunding the war is one of the most effective ways to force President Donald Trump to end the military portion of the war, with options like war powers resolutions unable to force his hand.

Some of the people not in support of the proposal, however, are top Democrats. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-New York) said last week that he opposes even the idea of barring funds from being used for the war, in favor of a war powers resolution that the Trump administration is likely to ignore. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-New York), facing a challenge to his leadership from one of the top Senate champions of the proposal to defund the war, has been mum on the issue.

The top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, Rosa DeLauro (Connecticut), has suggested that she does not want to use the continuing resolution to shut down the war.

“I think that the American people would like to see us end the war. I also believe that the American people may not believe that shutting the government down ends the war,” she said last week, her comments undercut by polling finding otherwise.

As Trump cracks down on political speech, independent media is increasingly necessary.

author: Arezu Fayyazi
title: Denied Education, Denied Choice: The Rise of Child Marriage in Afghanistan
content:
Five years after the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan, reports of child marriage are increasing. Globally, more than 12 million girls are married before the age of 18 every year. UN Women identifies education, legal protections, and social support as critical measures for preventing child marriage. Yet in Afghanistan, the Taliban have systematically dismantled these very protections. By banning girls from education beyond the sixth grade, restricting women’s participation in public life, and eliminating pathways to independence, the Taliban are leaving Afghan girls increasingly vulnerable to early and forced marriage.

The Taliban have created an environment in which women and girls are cut off from opportunities, resources, and support systems that would allow them to shape their own futures. With secondary schools and universities closed to girls, millions have lost access to higher education, professional opportunities, and the possibility of financial independence. Restrictions on women’s employment further compound this vulnerability, limiting their ability to support themselves and exercise control over decisions affecting their lives. In addition to these restrictions, the Taliban have issued over 160 decrees and directives affecting all aspects of Afghan girls’ and women’s lives.

The consequences of child marriage extend far beyond economic hardship. Marriage at an early age often forces girls into adulthood before they are physically, emotionally, or socially prepared. It can end their education, increase their exposure to domestic violence, and put them at greater risk of early pregnancy and serious maternal health complications. These risks are especially severe in Afghanistan, where women’s access to healthcare is increasingly threatened and limited by restrictions on female healthcare workers, women’s freedom of movement, and international aid organizations.

The loss of education is particularly consequential because schools provided far more than academic instruction. They offered girls a sense of community, a degree of protection, and access to trusted adults who could recognize abuse and intervene when necessary. Without these spaces, girls have fewer opportunities to seek help, build support networks, or challenge decisions made about their futures. The Taliban’s dismantling of legal protections, including the Ministry of Women’s Affairs and the removal of women from judicial positions, has further weakened the systems through which women and girls could seek protection and justice.

For Afghan girls, the fundamental right to decide when and whom to marry is increasingly constrained by circumstances beyond their control. The closure of schools, restrictions on employment, and dismantling of legal and social protections have steadily narrowed their choices. What should be decisions about their own lives and futures are increasingly shaped by a system designed to deny them agency and independence.

Preventing child marriage requires more than addressing individual cases. It means restoring the conditions that allow girls to remain in school, women to achieve financial independence, and all women and girls to exercise their rights and make decisions about their own lives. Until Afghan girls regain access to education, opportunity, and meaningful protection, the Taliban’s policies will continue to leave them increasingly vulnerable to early marriage and rob them of the freedom to grow and to determine their own futures.

Sources: Kabul Tribune, UNICEF, Afghanistan International, OHCHR

author: Dionne Phillips, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter
title: From bending time to 16 names for a berry — a poet finds inspiration in her ancestral languages
content:
Poet Kalli Van Stone’s new collection ‘welík’t’ was published in September. Submitted images


While exploring nsyilxcn (syilx language) and Secwepemctsín (Shuswap language) dictionaries, Kalli Van Stone (Spyu7) found herself drawn to words that held concepts she couldn’t find in English or Latin dictionaries.


In nsyilxcn, for example, she came across a word for the bending of time, which inspired her two-line poem “sumix kaʔɬis medicine power iii.”


These teachings opened up new worlds for Van Stone, which she began exploring through poetry.


Her debut poetry collection titled

welík’t

 — meaning “sparkle” in Secwepemctsín — was published

by Nightwood Editions

 in September.


The collection is divided into three sections: “nsyilxcn,” “english poems with indian names,” and “secwepemctsín.” Translations accompany her poems, alongside her own artwork.


Van Stone, who is syilx and Secwépemc from the north end of Okanagan Lake in “B.C.,” began reclaiming her ancestral languages a decade ago. This collection grew out of that work.


Across the collection’s 77 poems, Van Stone writes about personal experiences, the lives of her ancestors and the differences between her languages.


“They’re meant to be kind of shorter, more musical phrases, and then to kind of highlight any cool curiosities I find in the language,” she told IndigiNews.


‘I don’t let it stop me if I don’t have the words’


Van Stone is particularly drawn to words in nsyilxcn and Secwepemctsín that “challenge the Western concepts of time and personhood,” as well as those that speak to spirituality and ceremony.


Finding new words that displayed inspiring concepts brought up feelings of excitement and fulfilment for Van Stone. She references the nsyilxcn word kʷu ksq́ʷiɬq́ʷɬt, which translates to “you do wonders.” 


Dictionaries are only one place she looks for inspiration. Van Stone also draws on things she’s heard throughout her life, returning to them later when she sits down to write. 


“Mostly, it’ll just be like something cool I’ve heard throughout my life, and I’ll kind of tuck it away and then expand on it later in my own time,” she said.


“Or I find something really cool in the dictionary, or just in other documents or videos, and I’ll be like, ‘Whoa, there’s so much in that one sentence,’ and then I’ll kind of make my own thing.”


Writing in languages she’s still learning has, in part, shaped her aesthetic as a poet.


“I thought it was a really cool challenge to make something beautiful using some of the limitations I have. I know enough to do something creative, but it also makes it more simple, very stripped down to core ideas,” she said.


“I don’t let it stop me if I don’t have the words.”


There is also a musical quality to this brevity. In some of her poems, Van Stone experimented with call and response, drawing on musical traditions from her communities.


In the

notes accompanying her poem

 “nt̓aʔlils,” Van Stone draws a parallel between a drumstick striking a drum and a dancer’s feet striking the earth. She relates these movements to syilx teaching about working through different emotions. 


‘Our languages are sisters’


Van Stone has found similarities between nsyilxcn and Secwepemctsín, both members of the Salishan language family. 


“Our languages are sisters, so I love that there are so many ways where they kind of converge into each other, and then I was really interested in where they’re different,” she explained.


“Then we have really similar but still distinct music styles and a lot of our seasonal round is really similar, so that’s why it just felt so nice to learn both and do both and embrace all my ancestral sides.”


Working between nsyilxcn, Secwepemctsín and English brought its own challenges, particularly when translating and finding words that could convey what she wanted to express.


In “sixteen names of síyaʔ,” Van Stone lists 16 nsyilxcn names for the Saskatoon berry, compared with three English and Latin names. She connects that difference to the relationships her people have developed with the plant over thousands of years. She writes:


ʔupnkst uł taq̓mst skwists iʔ síya

sixteen names of siyaʔ


síyaʔ

sx̌wetl’x̌wítlaʔst

wusxenílheml̓x

t’et’k̓’ílhmel̓x

t’et’íkwt’ekwt

spep’aʕts’álak̓w

slhk̓ilhp

slhak̓

skw’lkw’lk̓in

sk̓w’ets’k̓w’ets’wiʔhálhaʔk̓

sk’ek’sálhaʔk̓

siʔílhp

siyíya

lhek̓’alhpákst

lexwús

kt’etíkws


how many names?

there are sixteen names


síyaʔ

serviceberry …

author: Valerie Anne
title: Liv Hewson Opens Up to Drew Barrymore About the Early Parts of Their Career
content:
feature image photo by The Drew Barrymore Show/Ash Bean via Getty Images

Yellowjackets star Liv Hewson reunited with their former Santa Clarita Diet co-star Drew Barrymore on Drew’s talk show this week.

In the interview, they discuss all sorts of topics, including but not limited to Yellowjackets, of course. Drew presents Liv with gifts for what she thought was their engagement, but Liv reveals that actually they got married already. (There are actually really cute pics that pop up behind them of the couple as well in the clip, so you should check it out.) Drew’s now-wedding gifts are two beautiful candlesticks Drew said represents the two of them living together in harmony.

Liv talks about meeting their now-spouse on the set of Yellowjackets when they were AD, and recounts seeing them for the first time and having a “who IS that” moment immediately.

Drew shows Liv a clip of another of their Santa Clarita Diet co-stars, Skyler Gisondo, asking Liv to share dating advice, and their advice boils down to the fact that people want to feel safe and that should be a priority in any relationship, not just romantic. (This is not really here nor there but I could listen to Liv talk for hours. They have such a calming presence and such a thoughtful way of speaking and you can tell, even just from little clips and interviews, that they are a deeply intelligent person, both intellectually and emotionally, and I just really love hearing them talk about pretty much anything.)

The pair also talks about Molly Ringwald coming on Yellowjackets to play Van’s mother, and Liv says they really hit the jackpot when it came to fictional moms, having now had two legends (Molly and Drew herself) play their mom on television.

Liv also talks about how they felt like they were living in a “defensive crouch” for a long time; they came to the US to work when they were 20 and felt like they had to go back in the closet as nonbinary when they started working in Hollywood, but that Drew and the cast of Santa Clarita Diet became a soft place for them to land and they are really grateful to her for that.

It’s a very sweet interview and as sad as I am to see Yellowjackets come to an end, I’m really excited to see what Liv will get up to next, mostly because they are extremely talented and should be cast in whatever the hell they want, but also because, selfishly, I want to watch them on more press tours.

+ Miley Cyrus also got married, to drummer Maxx Morando

+ Hunter Schafer is kicking ass and taking names in her new series, Bladerunner 2099

+ Speaking of Hunter Schafer, she said she tried polyamory but is more into monogamy; she supports it of course but says there’s too much scheduling for her

+ Jennifer Love Hewitt is going to reunite with I Know What You Did Last Summer costar Ryan Phillippe in an upcoming 911/911: Nashville crossover (I know this is a stretch to include here but both shows do have queer women on them and also J.Love was one of my roots so LET ME HAVE THIS)

author: Jonathan Pinckney
title: Rebuilding American democracy with resistance and relationships
content:
This article

Rebuilding American democracy with resistance and relationships

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


What comes next for American democracy? Our research into authoritarian regimes reveals a striking pattern in how autocracies begin to fall apart — and democracy starts to regain ground.


The 2026 U.S. midterms revealed deep and growing frustration with the Trump administration, including among communities that

have traditionally

 supported Republicans. The secretary of the army, a Trump appointee,

resigned

 after disputes over military readiness and the Iran war. Small businesses

sued

 the administration over tariffs, while companies denounced ICE raids for gutting profits. The CEO of the South Texas Builders Association, a three-time Trump voter,

attacked the administration

 over ICE raids, saying that “South Texas will never be red again.” On Nov. 3, his prediction came true as Texas border counties

saw historic swings

 toward the Democratic party. These signs reveal widening cracks in alliances that have kept Trump in power.


This expanding circle of dissent evokes a common global pattern: When compliance with an authoritarian leader begins to break down, it can trigger a cascade of opposition that ultimately leads to regime collapse. Brazilian businesses that backed Jair Bolsonaro eventually denounced his anti-democratic behaviors, contributing to his electoral defeat. When parts of the Catholic Church removed support from the far-right Law and Justice Party in Poland, its governing coalition fragmented. And in Hungary, the electoral coalition that brought down Prime Minister Viktor Orbán was led by defectors from Orbán’s own party.  


When and why do people stop complying with dictators? We studied the behavior of thousands of key social groups whose compliance is critical for dictatorships to remain in power. These include businesses, unions, security forces and faith groups, key pillars whose political, economic and moral resources keep regimes standing. Looking at dictatorships and backsliding democracies in the post-Cold War era, one clear pattern stands out: Broad civic mobilization

and

 dense social ties between those complying with the regime and members of a pro-democracy opposition encourages non-compliance. Mass noncompliance is how autocracies fall. Indeed, the

chances of stopping democratic backsliding

 while relying only on institutional channels like litigation, legislation and voting is about 7.5 percent. The presence of a broad-based civil resistance increases the probability of success to around 53 percent.  


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


Both broad mobilization and social connection are crucial because of the nature of compliance. While some people comply because of true ideological alignment, most do so for more ordinary reasons: to advance careers, protect business interests, show deference to authority, or out of simple psychological inertia. Others may for their safety. When people fear political retaliation, public support can mask private indifference or even opposition. For example, while farm bureaus across the U.S. may avoid publicly denouncing the administration, plenty of farmers and ranchers are

seething

. While big business has largely refrained from publicly criticizing the administration,

behind closed doors

 many CEOs are exasperated. A pro-democracy front should make room for people withdrawing their support for all of these reasons.  


Broad-based civic mobilization — where diverse groups use

protests

, marches,

boycotts

 and walkouts to push back — changes this picture. If people both see and believe that dissent is widespread, they are more likely to shift their behavior. Courage becomes contagious. 


Strong social ties between a regime’s pillars of support and its opponents can facilitate a cascade of dissent. If people only see those who are different from them protesting, their dissent is easy to dismiss as the actions of a radical few. Yet if those they know and trust begin to speak out, such actions are more difficult to discount. This helps explain why the

spread of protests

 into rural and traditionally conservative parts of the U.S. is noteworthy. In Tunisia’s “Jasmine Revolution,” the national labor union — initially a co-opted part of the Ben Ali dictatorship — shifted to supporting the revolution when local offices that had been regularly …

author: Unknown
title: ¡A la Huelga!: A Full Report on Spain’s General Strike from Vallekas, Madrid, and Barcelona
content:
In response to the violent eviction of Maricarmen Abascal, a disabled 87-year-old woman, people around Spain poured into the streets and set up

encampments

 in the plazas in a movement against evictions and gentrification. On November 11, a general strike took place throughout the country—the first in

fourteen years

. Here, we present accounts of the events from the vantage points of

Madrid

 and

Barcelona

.


This is a valuable document for all who seek to build the power to defend our communities.


The View from Madrid


We sit in a loosely arranged circle in a local social center run by a trade union. It’s just past midnight. When the clock strikes 12, marking the beginning of Wednesday, November 11, we erupt into cheers. Spain’s first general strike in 14 years is underway.


4.5 million people mobilized


1340 committees across the Spanish state


108 cities mobilized


4 million+ leaflets distributed


600,000+ posters put up


“General Strike for Housing” website


The building opened at 8 pm on Tuesday; it will stay open until 8 pm on Wednesday, with a room designated for strikers to take naps. People mill about, preparing food for our late dinner, drying wet clothing with a hairdryer that someone thought to bring from home. Some catch up with old friends, as the social center has become a gathering place for all in the area who need it. Others sign up to take shifts making coffee, preparing food, and protecting the space over the hours ahead.


We are

Vallekanos

, some by birth, others more recent transplants. Vallecas, known as Vallekas to many, is an urban area of Madrid so large that it was divided into two districts (Puente de Vallecas and Villa de Vallecas). The area is an epicenter of anti-fascist working-class resistance in Spain’s capital. After

Maricarmen was evicted

 in September and the general strike was announced in October, local organizations and social movements in the districts came together to help organize for the strike. Similar convergences have taken place in thousands of localities around Spain.


“It’s syndicalist terrorism.”


—Isabel Díaz Ayuso, right-wing President of the “Madrid Community”


The enthusiasm that fills this social center on the eve of the general strike flows from the same energy that erupted in millions of Spaniards on the day that Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old woman, was evicted from her home of 70 years in Madrid. Something clicked in the collective consciousness of the country at that moment. The percentage of Spain’s population that lives as tenants has risen steadily over the last few decades, reaching 25%, and recently, rents have skyrocketed.


All of us have heard the horror stories. A coworker who lives in a village a hundred kilometers away because they couldn’t afford housing near the office. Families with children who are forced to live in a single sub-letted room. Residents of protected housing who were evicted after their homes were sold to ruthless investment funds.


A memorial to Maricarmen a few steps away from her home.


Thanks to years of hard work by grassroots housing movements across the country, a voice has emerged to connect these struggles. The

Sindicato de Inquilinas

 (“Tenant’s Union”) has become a household name, appearing day after day in the news and on social media. The Union has shown the country that it is neither normal nor right that decent, stable housing has become increasingly impossible to find in this country, and the opportunity to become a homeowner even more so. The Union has exposed these struggles as the product of a deliberate political and financial strategy perpetrated by the wealthy. The Union has developed a powerful architecture of local assemblies, which made it possible to channel this collective outrage into a call for a general strike.


What follows is a local report and analysis from the districts of Vallekas and the city of Madrid as a whole, tracing the efforts leading up to the strike and the events of the day itself.


It Was About Time for a Strike!


As

we reported last month

, the current housing crisis in Spain had been approaching a breaking point in the months leading up to Maricarmen’s eviction. In Madrid, rental prices have risen 50% over the past five years, and many in the city find themselves forced to spend upwards of 70% of their monthly salaries on rent. In 2025, there were nearly 25,000 evictions nationwide, 74.6% of which were due to non-payment of rent …

author: Unknown
title: How the Riots Spread to Italy : An Account from the October 17 Uprising in Milan
content:
Across Europe, young people are rising up in rebellion. From

Spain

 and

France

 to Albania and even

Germany

, demonstrators are breaking with complacency and obedience and breaking through the constraints intended to control them.


This is reminiscent of the previous wave of unrest. In November 2018, the

Yellow Vest

 movement broke out in France, precipitating

several months

 of street conflict throughout the country. By fall of 2019, a global wave of uprisings was underway from

Hong Kong

,

Ecuador

, and

Chile

 to

Sudan

,

Catalunya

, and

Lebanon

. All this set the stage for the

George Floyd Rebellion

 to spread

around the United States

 in 2020.


It remains to be seen whether the wave of protest emanating from France today is indicative of a new groundswell of worldwide momentum—and it remains uncertain what it would take for these movements to address the fundamental problems of our time. Everywhere around the world, the movements of 2019 and 2020 reached an

impasse

 when they exhausted the force they could bring to bear in the streets and shifted instead to doomed electoral and reformist campaigns. The heroic failure of those powerful movements suggests that nothing short of a revolutionary transformation of our society can address the catastrophes that

capitalism

 and the consolidation of political power in the hands of autocrats are creating.


Hopefully, these upheavals can serve as laboratories in which a new generation of revolutionaries can experiment with methods for making profound change. In the following account, anarchists in Italy describe the moment in October 2026 at which the movement in Italy exceeded control.


Cracks in the Façade


In Italy, despite soaring prices, stagnating wages, and deteriorating schools and public services, the right-wing regime of Giorgia Meloni continues to ignore widespread misery while increasing military spending. Did they think we would not resist as wealthy elites attempt to loot our future?


This fall, cracks began to appear in the façade of the ruling order. On September 22 and 23 in Modena, about fifty young people organized themselves to loot supermarkets. They all walked in together and recorded footage of themselves taking whatever they wanted. Since the beginning of October, truck drivers across southern Italy have been blocking the roads and striking in protest against the rising price of diesel. For weeks, supermarkets in the south lay nearly empty.


As the ferment slowly grew, a call from a newly formed initiative called “Italia in piazza” [“Italy in the Squares”] circulated on social media. Anonymous chats on Telegram channels began to promote a date to mobilize against the high cost of living: October 17. The call was picked up on TikTok and Instagram and circulated widely. In Milan, the group called for a convergence in a city park. This contributed to swelling the ranks of protesters.


The protests of October 17 took an array of different forms in cities across the country. In Turin, Bergamo, and Milan, widespread unrest and looting indicated a political dimension rarely seen in Italy.


The demonstrators who assembled in Milan’s Piazza del Duomo on October 17 only traveled a few streets before the police blocked them. This would usually stop a protest in its tracks, but that day was different. Within the blocked group of approximately five hundred demonstrators, the energy remained strong. They chanted and threw themselves against the assembled cops, applying pressure until they finally broke through the police line and poured into the side streets. This time, the repressive maneuvers of the police failed, enabling anyone who so desired to join in the protest.


The following week, the Meloni regime called in the army to repress the demonstrations, which only infuriated people further. On October 30, a nationwide strike brought tens of thousands into the streets in over 40 cities around Italy. Since then, protests have continued around the country. But the uprisings of October 17 marked the turning point when masses of young people shattered the consumer spectacle in an explosion of looting and street fighting.


The following testimony reaches us from some participants in the unrest of October 17 and 18 in Milan.


Under the Madonnina


Gleaming atop the dome of Milan Cathedral, the famous golden statue of the Virgin Mary known as the Madonnina looms over a city in revolt. Beneath her gilded gaze, cobblestones fly at …

author: David S. D'Amato
title: La Via Libertaria all’egalitarismo
content:
Di

David S. D’amato

. Originale:

The Libertarian Road to Egalitarianism

, del 14 novembre 2014. Tradotto da

Enrico Sanna

.


Secondo uno

studio recente di Emmanuel Saez e Gabriel Zucman per l’Ufficio nazionale per la ricerca economica

, “

lo 0,1% delle famiglie [americane] possiede tanta ricchezza quanto il 90% meno ricco

”. Sempre secondo lo studio, la tanto declamata “ripresa” non ha raggiunto la classe media; i benefici sono andati alla cima della piramide.


Mentre una piccola frazione della popolazione ammassa gran parte della ricchezza nazionale, esperti e accademici accusano e offrono soluzioni. Com’è facile immaginare, si accusa il libero mercato di causare differenze crescenti di ricchezza e reddito. Fautori delle liberalizzazioni e del libero mercato, i libertari sono spesso accusati di vivere in un mondo di fantasia, di ignorare il problema della disuguaglianza.


Siamo noi stessi a farlo: quando si arriva al dunque, troppi si sentono a disagio, si difendono sostenendo che la disuguaglianza

non è

 un problema, e che bisogna invece vedere lo stile di vita o qualche altro parametro. “Il capitalismo è un bene per i poveri!” Invece i libertari dovrebbero accettare il semplice fatto che la disuguaglianza è un grosso problema.


Non dobbiamo vedere nella disuguaglianza un punto debole del discorso sulla libertà economica, o una questione irrisolvibile. Le attuali relazioni economiche non sono il risultato della libertà di scambio o della legittima proprietà privata. In fatto di disuguaglianza, la ragione sta dalla parte dei libertari. Libertà e eguaglianza sono di fatto complementari, si rafforzano reciprocamente: dalla prima deriva la seconda.


Anarchici individualisti come Lysander Spooner sostenevano che “ricchezza e povertà estreme” sono il risultato del “diritto positivo”, sostituiscono il diritto naturale con un diritto arbitrario, “danno vita a monopoli e privilegi”. Sotto il capitalismo, spiega, chi possiede un certo capitale ha un particolare potere economico che non ha niente a che vedere con la libertà di produrre, scambiare e competere. In un’ottica generale, l’intervento dello stato beneficia chi è ricco e ha appoggi politici, oltre alle élite che possono influire su chi scrive e applica le regole che tutti dobbiamo rispettare.


Il meccanismo non è perfetto, e per questo sopra il capitalismo monopolistico troviamo tutto uno strato di misure chiaramente intese a proteggere i lavoratori, i consumatori e i poveri. Ma nessuna di queste misure riesce a intaccare l’obiettivo di fondo dell’intervento statale, il quale espropria i legittimi proprietari e mette le masse al servizio dei datori di lavoro. L’obiettivo storico dello stato, in breve, è la lotta di classe permanente, l’uso del proprio potere per tenere al sicuro un’aristocrazia socioeconomica.


La sinistra istituzionale ha certamente ragione sull’uguaglianza, ma tende a sbagliare in fatto di libertà, diritti individuali e mercato. L’anarchismo di mercato è per la libertà

ma anche

 per l’uguaglianza, e vuole una società senza stato in cui la legge ultima sia la parità di libertà e autorità.


La vera competizione aperta è una forza che ha il potere di dissolvere e disperdere. I libertari dovrebbero smettere di giustificare le attuali sconcertanti disuguaglianze come se fossero il risultato del

laissez-faire

 e della sovranità individuale.


Le nostre traduzioni sono finanziate interamente da donazioni. Se vi piace quello che scriviamo, siete invitati a contribuire. Trovate le istruzioni su come fare nella pagina

Sostieni C4SS

:

https://c4ss.org/sostieni-c4ss

.

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: a14 – What’s fermenting underground – Jazz Dance with today’s zine scene
content:
Our collective can barely process all the correspondence coming our way. The least of which comes with scrappy limited edition zines. We endeavor to highlight them here when we can. Thankfully we have found a bright and wise ally who, when not tending to the garden warmly sits and reads deeply and widely freaky shit on paper. Maybe you will find a new life of reading zines, reviewing or even making them to thicken the plot we’re in.

Ear of Corn #66 24 pages – $2 foodfortunata@hotmail.com

It’s really endearing that even after 18 years, Ear of Corn still uses pasteup for the design, even as it’s moved to glossy paper. You can see on every page that Ear of Corn is still assembled old school and copied like we all used to do at Kinkos with glue sticks. The glue had a mild starchy taste, slightly sweet with a bitter finish; not unlike bad cheese pizza.

I have this conspiracy theory about this zine. I usually write reviews in batches, and I’ll often have multiple issues of Ear of Corn on my desk at a time. But I’ve never had any sequentially numbered issues. I’ve begun to suspect issues are not numbered non-sequentially or perhaps they are sequential, but aren’t printed in that order. Their practice of reviewing old and new releases side by side makes it impossible to know for sure; but they’re definitely up to something other than eating the glue.

Out From The Void #8 $5 – 70 pages outfromthevoid@yahoo.com

This issue goes places Out From The Void hasn’t gone before. The new topics are mostly adjacent to the core topic: the missing. So it’s the CAHOOTS program, police records requests, suicide, and police killings. But on page 51 begins a 6 page essay about Israel’s genocide in Gaza. It’s sober, historical and philosophical without trumpeting statistics.

In the middle of Issue #8 is a photo essay reprinted from the zine Here’s What I’ve Hidden Under My Tongue. Writer DJT was visiting an abandoned and mostly collapsed mental institution. In the introduction Brenton Gicker comments that he didn’t write any of the stories in this issue. I appreciate that Gicker puts his mission ahead of his ego to spread awareness of these topics but I do miss his voice as a writer. But until next time, we get more tales of the missing, the lost and the found.

The story of James B. Hunt and Fluke goes back to issue #16 of the infamous Fluke fanzine in 2018. Kudos if you kept that issue, it’s now a fine collectible. Even Maximum RockNRoll said so. They saw the future, perhaps even more clearly than I did. Gina Murrell always had a sixth sense for such things. But if you wake up feeling a bit goth, have a soft spot for monsters, or just like dead stuff, NXOEED might be for you.

If you don’t recognize his art that tells me you don’t skate bruh. His art appears on show flyers, album covers, websites, rad stickers and other greasy places. But among all that ephemera this issue is special. Usually Mr. Hunt lets the ink speak for him, but this time we actually get a few precious pages of text; our first sense of the man himself. He’s a geezer, like me, trying to do punk rock things, but to also go to bed on time. I feel that in my soul.

$20 – 192 pages inequitypress@hotmail.com

It’s hard to say that many poets are famous today. But as poets go, some of those published in Big Hammer are highfalutin people now like David Cope, Donald Lev, Chris Stroffolino, Ken Greenley, and Enid Dame (RIP). Others, like Michael Pingarron, are still writing for Big Hammer. They’ve found their layer of strata, and one would hope some sense of belonging.

The first issue of Big Hammer rolled off the press in 1988. That was 38 years ago, kids. Statistically most of you reading this weren’t even born yet. That zine was way underground, like the Lincoln Tunnel; like the FDR Train Car in the pitch blackness of Track 61 marooned below Grand Central since 1945. But Dave Roskos is still out there in the tunnels, in the darkness, still editing and publishing Big Hammer. He’s doing it his own way, and accountable to no one. Doesn’t it sound grand?

Zine content from the eighties makes more sense in the context of its contemporary punk 7-inches” like “Too scared to be queer,” “Be a Fag,” and “Forbidden Love.” So I queued up the Homocore Hit parade cassette, and pondered its place in history. Homocore ran for just 7 issues between 1988 and 1991. If you didn’t catch my drift, it tapped into two communities which still remain the core of the underground today: queers and …

author: Admin101
title: Announcing Black Rose/Rosa Negra Locals in Austin, New York City, and Chicago
content:
We’re thrilled to announce the formation of three new Locals of Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation (BRRN)! From the Texas Hill Country, to the Great Lakes, to the Northeast, our organization is growing deeper roots and expanding our capacity to organize, struggle, and build popular power in communities across the country.


As you will read below, each new local grows out of its members’ deep involvement in the popular struggles of their neighborhoods, workplaces, and broader communities. What follows are brief introductions in their members’ own words — including their contact info and social media handles.


Austin, TX


The Austin Local has officially re-formed! Our members are primarily focused on labor and tenant organizing, as well as rapid response to ICE. We are also making preparations for an open reading group to discuss

BRRN’s Program

.


We welcome those with interest to contact us.


Email:

 austin@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_atx


Chicago, IL


The Chicago local is back! Our logo honors the Haymarket Martyrs Memorial — a symbol of the organizers who made anarchism a powerful current in immigrant and women workers’ struggles of their time, as well as the place we gathered for our first event all together as a local. 


We carry their memory with us alongside others as we work in the social movements where we are rooted. These include tenant struggles on the South and Northwest sides, as well as labor organizing in the Chicago Teachers Union. We look forward to deepening our connections with comrades in our movements and others through collective study and struggle.


Email:

 chicago@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:


@blackrose_chicago

 


New York City, NY


Members of the New York City Local organize with tenants, neighbors, youth, coworkers, and parents to build Black, Brown, and working-class popular power throughout the city. Sites of social insertion include the Astoria Tenant Union in Queens, anticarceral youth and parent programs in Manhattan, immigrant defense coalitions in Brooklyn, the American Association of University Professors, and more. True to BRRN’s internationalist character, we also organize within the Palestinian and Sudanese solidarity movements.


From the Young Lords to Occupy Wall Street, we recognize the integral role that revolutionaries in NYC have played in past freedom struggles and look forward to reviving organized anarchism in the especifista tradition across the five boroughs.

BRRN’s Program

 serves as a blueprint for renewed efforts to confront imperial and capitalist violence as anarchist militants living at the nexus of US empire and global capital .


Email:

 nyc@blackrosefed.org

Instagram:

 @blackrose_nyc


Are you organizing at your workplace, on your campus, or in your neighborhood? Looking for a political home in which you can strategize with others about how to build power, force concessions, and push our mass movements in a revolutionary direction?


Black Rose/Rosa Negra could be right for you.


Read our

Join

 page and send us a membership inquiry!

Announcing Black Rose/Rosa Negra Locals in Austin, New York City, and Chicago

Black Rose/Rosa Negra Anarchist Federation

.

author: CMI Argentina
title: Milton Tolomeo suspendió su huelga de hambre
content:
El preso político Milton Tolomeo, encarcelado por haber participado del rechazo popular contra la regresiva reforma laboral, suspendió la medida tras lograr una serie de conquistas en favor de todo su pabellón.


Compartimos el comunicado de la Coordinadora por la libertad de lxs presxs políticxs:


Milton suspende su huelga de hambre


Luego de haber sostenido dos semanas de huelga de hambre, Milton Tolomeo, preso por haber participado de la movilización popular contra la reforma laboral, decidió suspender la medida porque logró una serie de conquistas en favor de todo su pabellón.


Los detenidos del módulo 4 sector A3B derecho interpusieron un Habeas Corpus Colectivo Correctivo para exigir mejoras en las condiciones de alojamiento del Complejo Penitenciario Federal nº VIII al que fueron trasladados.


A través de este recurso y de otras gestiones judiciales, y tras una audiencia con el Juzgado Federal de Morón, representantes de distintos sectores del personal del complejo se entrevistaron con Milton y se comprometieron a garantizar la puesta en marcha de sus reclamos: acceso a la salud, derecho de estudiar y trabajar, restitución de pertenencias, provisión de agua potable, etcétera.


Es por ello que Milton aceptó suspender por el momento la medida de fuerza, supeditado a que todo lo informado por las autoridades judiciales y penitenciarias se cumpla. Caso contrario, retomará la huelga.


Nuestro compañero está entero, se siente bien de salud y a la espera de que el Servicio Penitenciario cumpla lo que se comprometió a hacer.


Una vez más, decimos todos juntos que luchar sirve.

author: La Zarzamora
title: Va cayendo el Montaje hacia familia de Julia Chuñil, rechazan pruebas que sustentan la hipótesis de la fiscalía
content:
Ya van más de dos años de búsqueda de la verdad por parte de la familia de Julia Chuñil Catricura. En todo este tiempo han enfrentado un proceso judicial en el que la fiscalía a cargo de Tatiana Ezquivel, luego negligencias y un proceso bastante tardío, con diferentes operativos denigrantes, hostigamiento, cambios de fiscal, intimidación y apremios ilegítimos ha mantenido a la familia soportando hasta hoy la violencia estatal histórica hacia las personas oprimidas. Generando, por supuesto, secuelas psicológicas y un profundo daño.

La hipótesis de Fiscalía se centró en la familia de la lamuen, la cual armaron con pruebas que se han ido cayendo con el paso de los meses, culpando a los propios hijos de asesinarla y desaparecerla. Los medios orquestados por la Elite no dudaron en hacer viral la noticia, ayudando a generar aún más criminalización, y un juicio social sin pruebas contundentes hacia los hijos.

Ya van diez meses de que apresaron a todos los hijos y al yerno de Julia – al cual hicieron testificar sin abogado presente en donde declara la supuesta culpabilidad de uno de los Hijos que hoy sigue tras las rejas-. Con el paso del tiempo, es el mismo yerno quién desmiente su propia declaración denunciando amenazas de parte de la fiscalía para testificar en contra de la familia. Otro de los testigos es protegido y se ha cuestionado por varias razones la legitimidad de esta declaración.

Sumado a lo anterior en la última audiencia del 20 de noviembre del 2026 se cae otra de las pruebas de fiscalía, ya que los estudios de los supuestos ‘’huesos humanos’’ de los que alardeo tanto la prensa y los abogados termino siendo completamente desechada por haberse comprobado que eran osamentas de animales.

Audio de la Abogada Karina Riquelme defensora de la Familia de Julia Chuñil tras la audiencia el 20 de noviembre en los Lagos:

Por otro lado, organizaciones denuncian un trasfondo político por tres razones, la primera y la más importante, el mayor sospechoso es perteneciente a las familias más poderosas de $hile: Juan Carlos Morstad Anwanterd, este hombre estuvo relacionado a la tierra por años a través de CONADI, por sus negocios agrícolas y forestales, y por otro lado también es bien sabido que la justicia en $hile funciona con poder y dinero, demostrándose en cómo han sido los tratos hacia quien también es imputado. De hecho según el Medio de Comunicación Contrapoder Chile »…tuvo acceso a un documento que confirma que Fiscalía citó al empresario Juan Carlos Morstadt, a declarar en calidad de imputado; luego que un informe de la PDI detectara contradicciones entre su ubicación y el tráfico de su teléfono en noviembre de 2024.»

Segundo, la abogada Tatiana Ezquivel estuvo relacionada a otras investigaciones de asesinato a defensoras de la tierra, específicamente en el caso del asesinato de Macarena Valdes. En este caso la fiscalía negó el presunto asesinato y mantuvo la hipótesis de supuesto suicidio por parte de la Lamuen. La misma abogada que hoy mantiene preso a uno de los hijos, tubo 10 años a la familia de Macarena en un limbo el cual también esconde empresarios latifundistas interesados en instalar sus empresas y destruir los territorios. Y Tercero, en $hile la Elite económica funciona a través de la desaparición de personas, sicariato y asesinato de los y las defensoras de la Tierra para concretar sus proyectos extractivistas.

Dejamos la declaración publicada este 24 de noviembre por la Familia de Julia:

COMUNICADO FAMILIA JULIA CHUÑIL

En la reciente audiencia de revisión de medidas cautelares el Juzgado de Garantía de los Lagos resolvió mantener la prisión preventiva de Javier Troncoso, quien cumple 10 meses privado de libertad.

En dicha instancia se presentó formalmente el informe técnico emitido por el Servicio Médico Legal (SML). En razón de la rigurosidad técnica y científica con que el organismo forense realizó sus análisis antropométricos y de laboratorio, el informe concluye de manera objetiva la desestimación de osamentas humanas en el predio habitacional de la familia, confirmando el origen animal de los restos analizados.

Dada la validez técnica acreditada por el SML, la familia ha resuelto solicitar formalmente que peritos especializados del propio Servicio Médico Legal lleven a cabo un conjunto de nuevas diligencias investigativas. El objetivo prioritario es avanzar en la búsqueda de nuestra madre y abuela Julia del Carmen Chiuñil Catricura con estándares científicos rigurosos.

author: Darío Aranda
title: Ley de Tierras: vía libre para desalojos exprés y un Congreso a medida del extractivismo
content:
OPINIÓN


Por Silvina Ramírez*


Finalmente, se sancionó la Ley de Inviolabilidad de la Propiedad Privada. El Senado la convirtió en ley, luego de múltiples avatares que tuvieron su epicentro en la extranjerización de la tierra. La derogación de un artículo del polémico DNU 70/23, que eliminó la Ley de Tierras Rurales —la que impuso un límite a la extranjerización— fue el punto de partida de un enorme debate público que culminó con esta última sanción.


El bochornoso papel de la

Corte Suprema de Justicia de la Nación

, que en el lapso de diez días puso en vigencia el artículo en cuestión suspendiendo una medida cautelar, y luego en un golpe de timón volvió a establecer dicha medida prohibiendo otra vez la extranjerización, concluye en un acto final de sanción de una ley que incluye la restitución de la Ley 26.737 de tierras rurales.


Sintetizar en un párrafo las idas y vueltas parlamentarias y las decisiones de la Corte Suprema no fue una tarea fácil. Sí traduce el nivel de “tironeo” político, las negociaciones desenfrenadas, decisiones judiciales de la máxima instancia del país inexplicables, y la relevancia de

la movilización

 de diversos sectores sociales que presionaron para preservar la soberanía. En pocas palabras,

se logró la restitución de una ley que protege el territorio de la injerencia externa

.


Sin embargo, la movilización popular no alcanzó para frenar los desalojos exprés y la restricción para las expropiaciones, que subsisten en el texto de la Ley de Inviolabilidad de la propiedad privada aprobada. Estas medidas perjudican a vastos sectores de la sociedad, entre ellos las comunidades indígenas.


Los desalojos apuntan tanto a inmuebles urbanos como rurales. Al agilizar el proceso y acortar los plazos, la fragilidad de aquellos potenciales desalojados se agudiza. En el caso de las comunidades indígenas, la seguidilla de desalojos o intentos de desalojos que se dieron en los últimos meses —algunos de ellos pudieron ser suspendidos—, bajo la vigencia de esta ley, adquieren mayor gravedad.


Es el caso también de las expropiaciones. Aquellas comunidades indígenas que tienen expectativas de recuperar sus territorios a través de un procedimiento administrativo como lo es la expropiación, van a encontrar ahora muchas más dificultades, por lo que una de las vías posibles de titulación colectiva encuentra nuevos obstáculos. Nada es fácil para las comunidades indígenas que pretenden gozar de sus derechos territoriales reconocidos.


Esta ley debe leerse a la luz de otras medidas de este Gobierno que privilegian no sólo la propiedad privada, sino las inversiones extranjeras, despreciando e invisibilizando el reclamo legítimo de las comunidades indígenas, campesinos y trabajadores rurales, entre ortos. El

Régimen de Incentivo para Grandes Inversiones (RIGI)

, la derogación de la

Ley 26.160 (Emergencia Territorial Indígena)

, el

desguace de la Ley de Glaciares

, el rol nefasto del Instituto Nacional de Asuntos Indígenas (INAI), son

piezas de una maquinaria al servicio de la explotación de los bienes comunes naturales y el despojo

, otra vez, de los territorios indígenas.


Es cierto que se logró frenar la extranjerización de la tierra, debido principalmente a la presión ciudadana. No obstante, los objetivos de esta gestión de gobierno son claros. Muchas veces se retrocede para avanzar con mayor fuerza. Es imprescindible estar alertas frente a potenciales avances que pretendan erosionar aún más la ya débil institucionalidad pública y seguir socavando derechos que costaron tanto obtener. Que la arena (o la cal) no tape la cal (o la arena).


*

Especialista en Derechos Indígenas. Docente de la Facultad de Derecho de la UBA. Miembro de la Asociación de Abogados/as de Derecho Indígena (AADI).


La entrada

Ley de Tierras: vía libre para desalojos exprés y un Congreso a medida del extractivismo

 se publicó primero en

Agencia de Noticias Tierra Viva

.

author: James Green
title: Donald Trump contra ataca
content:
Trump e seus apoiadores do movimento MAGA (

Make America Great Again

) ainda estão atordoados com a derrota histórica sofrida em 3 de novembro.

A partir de 3 de janeiro de 2027, o partido Democrata irá controlar a Câmara dos Representantes — que corresponde à nossa Câmara dos Deputados — com 257 cadeiras contra 171 dos republicanos (7 vagas ainda estão em aberto). Os democratas também terão uma maioria de 56 a 44 no Senado.


No dia seguinte ao “

tsunami democrata

” que alterou a correlação de forças nos EUA, Trump permanecia em total negação quanto ao resultado. Em vez de falar à imprensa sobre o que acabara de acontecer, o “decorador-chefe” da Casa Branca conduziu os jornalistas em

um tour

 pelas suas “reformas residenciais”.


Com detalhes minuciosos, Trump descreveu a grandiosidade de seu salão de festas dourado. Em seguida, exaltou o novo heliponto instalado nos jardins da Casa Branca, a remodelação do Jardim das Rosas (Rose Garden) e os preparativos para a construção do “

Arco de Trump

” — uma estrutura de cerca de 76 metros de altura que irá projetar sua sombra sobre o Cemitério Nacional de Arlington. Esse local serve como local de repouso para mais de 400 mil veteranos de guerra, militares da ativa e seus dependentes elegíveis, além de abrigar os restos mortais do presidente assassinado John F. Kennedy e de membros de sua família.


Dois dias depois, Trump concedeu uma entrevista, aparentemente reflexiva, ao programa jornalístico televisivo “

60 Minutes

”, na qual reconheceu que a guerra no Irã, o alto custo de vida e as medidas extremas contra imigrantes foram fatores que levaram à vitória surpreendente dos democratas. Ele defendeu, contudo, que, se seu nome estivesse na cédula, os republicanos teriam derrotado os democratas. Seus opositores argumentam que o público votou contra os republicanos justamente para repudiar Trump.


Em seguida, menos de uma hora após a gravação da entrevista, o presidente mudou de postura.

Em vez de enviar uma mensagem conciliadora aos seus opositores, anunciou que seu novo chefe de gabinete seria

Steven Miller

 — assessor presidencial responsável pelas políticas imigratórias draconianas de Trump e conhecido por sua hostilidade e desdém em relação aos democratas no Congresso. Pouco depois, os republicanos na Câmara dos Representantes escolheram o radical de direita

Jim Jordan

 como novo líder da minoria, sinalizando que Trump mantém um controle firme sobre seu partido no Congresso.


O aperto de Trump no controle do partido Republicano


A dimensão da derrota eleitoral dos republicanos — que perderam

disputas

 em estados com inclinação republicana ou considerados decisivos (“estados-pêndulo”), como Alasca, Carolina do Sul, Geórgia, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Mississippi e Texas — não parece ter desencorajado os apoiadores fiéis de Trump. Ele e seus apoiadores não parecem compreender por que os eleitores rejeitaram, de forma avassaladora, os candidatos republicanos.


E como Trump não demonstrou qualquer desejo de buscar um consenso com os democratas sobre medidas para enfrentar algumas das questões que levaram a um comparecimento recorde às urnas, a maioria dos republicanos permanece relutante em criticar a Casa Branca. Em vez disso, eles correm para nomear o maior número possível de aliados fiéis de Trump para cargos no Judiciário e para aprovar leis impopulares antes de perderem a maioria no Congresso no próximo ano.


Uma exceção notável foi J. D. Vance, um dos possíveis pré-candidatos republicanos à presidência em 2028. Aproveitando-se do comentário de Trump sobre a oposição dos eleitores à guerra no Irã,

Vance sugeriu

 que esse foi um fator relevante para os fracassos eleitorais de Trump.


Isso não agradou ao presidente, que, após a crítica velada de Vance à Casa Branca, prontamente o excluiu das negociações sobre a guerra da Rússia contra a Ucrânia. Em vez disso, o vice-presidente foi incumbido de monitorar supostos

casos de corrupção

 em redutos democratas. E embora Trump pareça ter recuado em sua atitude de escantear Vance, nenhum outro republicano de destaque, seja no governo ou no Congresso, ousou criticar o presidente.


Democratas na ofensiva


Durante a campanha eleitoral, os candidatos democratas mantiveram o foco em

duas questões fundamentais

: o alto custo de vida e a responsabilidade do governo com as finanças do país.

author: anred
title: Sobre «Gordon», la ficción y la historia
content:
«Gordon» tiene oficio: una gran actuación, una atmósfera lograda, un ritmo que no afloja. Por eso importa discutir qué historia cuenta. Y, sobre todo, cuál deja afuera. ¿Dónde quedan el Cordobazo, el sindicalismo clasista, las comisiones internas, el Villazo, las huelgas, la radicalización estudiantil? No eran el decorado de una guerra entre aparatos. Eran parte de una irrupción obrera y popular que discutía quién mandaba en las fábricas, en las calles, en el país y en la vida. Las organizaciones revolucionarias tampoco eran una sola cosa. Tenían tradiciones, proyectos, estrategias y desacuerdos profundos sobre la lucha armada y su relación con ese movimiento de masas. No se trata de exigirle a una ficción que sea un manual de historia. Se trata de advertir cuándo sus licencias dejan de iluminar una época y empiezan a achicarla.

Por Fernando Rosso (La Izquierda Diario).


En su primera clase sobre Borges, Piglia invertía la pregunta: el problema no es cómo entra la realidad en la ficción, sino cómo la ficción se mete en la realidad. En «Tlön», el mundo imaginario termina invadiendo el verdadero. Algo parecido pasa cuando la ficción ocupa la memoria.


«Gordon» tiene oficio: una gran actuación, una atmósfera lograda, un ritmo que no afloja. Por eso importa discutir qué historia cuenta. Y, sobre todo, cuál deja afuera.


El primer recorte transforma la convulsión revolucionaria de los años setenta en operaciones clandestinas, secuestros, internas y venganzas. El segundo reduce la historia de las organizaciones político-militares a una sola trayectoria, la de Montoneros. Dos movimientos de cámara y un país entero queda fuera de cuadro.


¿Dónde quedan el Cordobazo, el sindicalismo clasista, las comisiones internas, el Villazo, las huelgas, la radicalización estudiantil? No eran el decorado de una guerra entre aparatos. Eran parte de una irrupción obrera y popular que discutía quién mandaba en las fábricas, en las calles, en el país y en la vida.


Las organizaciones revolucionarias tampoco eran una sola cosa. Tenían tradiciones, proyectos, estrategias y desacuerdos profundos sobre la lucha armada y su relación con ese movimiento de masas.


El secuestro de Oberdan Sallustro, en 1972, condensa el problema. Fue una operación del ERP. Pero la serie incorpora a militantes montoneros en el secuestro. Parece una licencia menor. Si todo empieza y termina en Montoneros, las diferencias políticas se borran y el pasado se vuelve un escenario poblado por guerrilleros intercambiables.


No se trata de exigirle a una ficción que sea un manual de historia. Se trata de advertir cuándo sus licencias dejan de iluminar una época y empiezan a achicarla.


Porque si los setenta se cuentan apenas como un duelo entre organizaciones armadas y represores, desaparecen las razones sociales y políticas de aquella rebelión. Y también se vuelve más difícil entender por qué hubo que desplegar semejante maquinaria de terror para aplastarla.


La ficción se mete en la realidad, decía Piglia. La pregunta es qué memoria va dejando cuando se apaga la pantalla.


Fuente:

https://www.laizquierdadiario.com/Sobre-Gordon-la-ficcion-y-la-historia

author: Rizomatica
title: Seis en huelga en la cárcel, en sus casas un gran nudo en las gargantas
content:
Revisando hoy las redes sociales me entero de que seis de los dieciocho condenados por el caso Molino Grollmus iniciaron una huelga de hambre seca en la cárcel de Biobío. Uno de ellos es José Melgarejo Calbullanca, a quien represento. La noticia me golpea, porque de todo lo que he visto de la cárcel aplicada a los mapuche, lo más duro, sin duda, es la huelga. Duro para el preso y duro para su familia, porque no solo deja de alimentarse el huelguista: les aseguro que la garganta de sus mujeres y de sus madres difícilmente traga, de solo saber que allá adentro los suyos están dispuestos a morir por justicia.


Por:

Daniela Sierra

, Abogada.


Una huelga no es una medida de presión, ni una puesta en escena. Sin agua, el cuerpo empieza a apagarse en días, no en semanas. A eso no se llega por cálculo; se llega cuando ya no quedan puertas que golpear.


¿Qué piden? Lo primero, que se anule un juicio en que se condenó con testigos que nadie vio. Así de simple. En el caso de José, dos de los testigos con identidad reservada nunca pisaron la sala: la Fiscalía renunció a ellos, y lo que supuestamente dijeron lo contaron unos policías, de oídas. Los jueces no les vieron la cara, la defensa no pudo hacerles una sola pregunta, y con eso a José le dieron más de ochenta años de cárcel.


La Convención Americana garantiza a todo acusado el derecho a interrogar a quien lo acusa (art. 8.2 f), y el Código Procesal Penal obliga a condenar solo con la prueba rendida en el juicio (art. 340). La Corte Interamericana ya se lo dijo a Chile en 2014, y en un caso mapuche, Norín Catrimán: no se puede condenar únicamente o en grado decisivo con testigos de identidad reservada. Y eso era con testigos que al menos declararon. Aquí, ni eso.


Tampoco se pide impunidad, como tanto les gusta repetir. Si la Corte Suprema anula, la ley ordena un juicio nuevo (art. 386 del Código Procesal Penal), esta vez con las reglas del juego, y si la prueba no alcanza, la absolución. Eso se resuelve el jueves en la Corte Suprema, que es donde se tiene que resolver; no en La Moneda ni en ninguna reunión con ministros.


Lo segundo que piden huele, para algunos, a privilegio: un módulo para presos mapuche en Biobío, que puedan entrar la machi y el logko, comer su comida, vestir su ropa, hablar chedungun, tener trabajo y talleres. Privilegio, dicen, como si rezar, comer lo propio y hablar la lengua de la abuela fueran lujos de hotel.


Pero el Convenio 169 de la OIT, vigente en Chile desde 2009, obliga a proteger las prácticas espirituales de los pueblos indígenas (art. 5), a considerar su cultura cuando se les impone una pena (art. 10) y a darles una salud que respete su propia medicina (art. 25). Las Reglas Mandela de Naciones Unidas exigen respetar las creencias de cada preso, ofrecerle educación y trabajo, y permitirle practicar su fe con alguien de su propia tradición (reglas 2, 4, 65 y 66). Y el Reglamento de Establecimientos Penitenciarios dice algo que debería bastar: fuera de los derechos que la condena le quita, el preso conserva la misma condición jurídica que cualquier ciudadano libre (art. 2).


Lo más curioso es que nada de esto es nuevo. Gendarmería informó a la Corte de Apelaciones de Temuco que su módulo de comuneros tiene encomiendas con alimentación culturalmente pertinente, acceso a lawen, medicina tradicional y machi, y talleres de trabajo. Es decir, lo que se pide en Biobío ya existe en Temuco. Entonces la pregunta no es por qué regalarles un privilegio, sino por qué un mapuche pierde derechos según la cárcel a la que lo manden.


El Estado tiene a estos seis hombres bajo su custodia y responde por su vida. Pero la salida no está en sentarse a mirar cuánto aguanta el cuerpo. Está en que la Corte Suprema aplique el estándar que ya se le impuso a Chile.


Lo que piden es juicio justo, no impunidad. Lo mínimo, eso que la humanidad ya pagó con demasiada sangre. Y que, mientras tanto, allá afuera, sus mujeres, sus madres, puedan volver a respirar a la espera del futuro abrazo de los suyos.


*Enviado a la radio


Esta información se publicó en

Radio Kurruf

.
