author: CMI Argentina
title: ¿Cuánto aguanta el dólar barato?
content:
El salto del riesgo país volvió a poner bajo presión al esquema cambiario. Economistas advierten sobre las tensiones de las bandas y el costo de sostener la divisa estable. ¿Ya nadie confía en el plan de Milei?


24/11/2026


La tensión financiera volvió a trasladarse al mercado cambiario. El 20, “viernes negro”, el riesgo país superó los 1.000 puntos básicos, para llegar este martes 24 hasta su máximo anual de 1.100, y el dólar registró nuevas subas en sus distintas cotizaciones, en jornadas marcadas por la caída de los bonos argentinos en Wall Street.


El movimiento expone las dudas de los inversores sobre el programa financiero del Gobierno, la capacidad de acumular reservas y la sostenibilidad del esquema económico de cara a 2027.


Los números del viernes negro


El indicador que elabora JP Morgan trepó hasta los 1.038 puntos, luego de avanzar 103 en un día, lo que lo colocó en su nivel más alto desde octubre de 2025. En paralelo, los bonos argentinos perdieron en promedio un 3,5% en la plaza neoyorquina y acumularon una baja semanal del 6%. En lo que va del año, los precios de la deuda argentina en dólares retrocedieron, en promedio, un 17%.


La presión también se reflejó en el mercado cambiario. El dólar mayorista cerró en $1.579, mientras que el minorista llegó a $1.595 en el Banco Nación. Entre las cotizaciones financieras, el MEP alcanzó los $1.676 y el contado con liquidación (CCL), los $1.782. La brecha entre este último y el tipo de cambio mayorista se ubicó en torno al 13%, el registro más elevado desde octubre del año pasado.


Sin pausa después del feriado


Luego del fin de semana extendido por el feriado trasladado del Día de la Soberanía, este martes el dólar minorista superó los $1.615 en el Banco Nación y el mayorista subió a $1.593. En cuanto a los tipos de cambios financieros, el CCL se disparó más de 5% y cotiza cercano a los $1.800, con una brecha de más del 13% frente al mayorista; mientras que el MEP llegó a operar arriba de los $1.705.


Las causas


El contexto internacional explica sólo en parte la situación vernácula, que es por demás preocupante.


Como consecuencia de la apertura económica del modelo Milei-Caputo, el mercado argentino quedó expuesto a cualquier cimbronazo puertas afuera. En este marco, los retrocesos en Wall Street y las tasas estadounidenses en alza afectaron con mayor fuerza a los mercados emergentes.


Pero las dudas también tienen raíces locales: la desaceleración de las compras de divisas del Banco Central, las necesidades de financiamiento y la incertidumbre política cuando comienza a acercarse el calendario electoral de 2027 hicieron lo suyo.


Las compras netas de dólares del BCRA promediaron apenas 32 millones diarios durante noviembre, hasta el día 13. La cifra contrasta con los 66 millones de octubre y los 77 millones de promedio diario acumulados en lo que va del año.


Las expectativas


La preocupación no se limita a los vencimientos inmediatos. El analista Emilio Botto, del grupo Mills Capital, señaló en declaraciones a

Infobae

 que en enero el Tesoro deberá afrontar pagos por unos 4.500 millones de dólares a tenedores privados de bonos y que, según estimaciones de economistas del mercado local, las necesidades adicionales de financiamiento para todo 2027 podrían alcanzar al menos los 8.000 millones. También advirtió que algunas fuentes de divisas que estuvieron disponibles este año podrían no repetirse con la misma magnitud.


Parece que el mercado no está dispuesto a seguir sosteniendo el dólar barato que quiere el gobierno.


Flotar es una cosa. Que se los lleven puestos (con Cepo) y tengan que dejarlo subir es otra…


— Carlos Rodriguez (@carod2015)

November 20, 2026


La tensión financiera puede trasladarse, además, al crédito y la actividad. En los próximos días vencen títulos en pesos por unos 25 billones; en diciembre, por 37 billones, y en enero, por 42 billones. La consultora LCG considera que el Tesoro podría renovar esos compromisos, aunque probablemente deba convalidar tasas más altas. Ese encarecimiento repercute sobre el financiamiento de empresas y familias y puede profundizar el freno económico.


Los economistas también pusieron el foco en las tensiones del propio esquema cambiario. En su cuenta de X, Mariano Calixto Fernández, examigo de Javier Milei, cuestionó la regla que ajusta las bandas cambiarias según la inflación pasada: “El Gobierno cometió el error de atrasar el tipo de cambio para bajar la inflación de forma …

author: Unknown
title: ISIS attacks military bus in Deir ez-Zor
content:
The Islamic State (ISIS) militant group has attacked a bus carrying personnel from the Syrian Ministry of Defense in the eastern Syrian province of Deir ez-Zor. The attack took place in al-Baghouz, once ISIS’s last territorial stronghold in Syria.


According to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights, the attack triggered armed clashes between ISIS militants and government forces. Both sides reportedly suffered casualties, with people killed and injured. No precise casualty figures were initially provided.

title: NPA-Mindoro reports failed AFP attack, 4 gov’t casualties
content:
The New People’s Army (NPA) reported the death of four government troopers in a clash at Bulalacao, Oriental Mindoro on Monday, thwarting a 1

st

 Infantry Battalion-Philippine Army strike operation.


The NPA said a unit of its Lucio de Guzman Command successfully defended itself against the raid at its temporary encampment in Sitio Gatol, Barangay San Roque, withdrawing safely after the firefight.


An ABS-CBN report of the incident quoted 203rd Infantry Brigade-Philippine Army commander Brig. Gen. Melencio Ragudo claiming only two soldiers were wounded and are at a stable condition at a hospital. The report also stated that said the clash started at around 8:35 AM.


The NPA, however, said civilians who were at the scene after the encounter reported that four soldiers were killed. The Red army likewise refuted 1st IB’s claim that firearms and equipment were seized from the guerillas.


The NPA added that its fighters spotted the approaching soldiers and opened fire on them before they could reach the camp.NPA-Mindoro spokesperson Madaay Gasic said their latest victory against the Armed Forces of the Philippines demonstrate the Red army’s will to fight and the people’s “unwavering support.” Gasic also belied Ragudo’s claim civilians tipped off the miitary about the NPA’s presence in the area.


“The people of Bulalacao and all the people of Mindoro celebrate the heroic resistance of their army against the enemy,” Gasic said. #

(Raymund B. Villanueva)

Serokê Herêma Kurdistanê bi matmayî û dilgiraniyeke kûr ve daxuyaniya Berdevkê Fermandarê Giştî yê Hêzên Çekdar ên Iraqê şermezar kir û ragihand ku di demekê de ku danûstandinên Hewlêr û Bexdayê ji bo çareserkirina pirsgirêkên hilawistî berdewam in, bikaranîna zimanê leşkerî tu pirsgirêkê çareser nake û di berjewendiya Iraqê û tu aliyekî de nîne. Serok Nêçîrvan Barzanî tekez kir ku Herêma Kurdistanê wekî hevbeşeke sereke di avakirina Iraqa nû de, piştgiriya parastina samanên niştimanî û cîbicîkirina yasayê dike, lê peywendiyên Hewlêr - Bexda divê li ser bingeha destûrê, rêzgirtina ji qewareya destûrî ya Herêma Kurdistanê û bingehên hevbeşî û têgihiştinê be, û hêz û aramiya Herêma Kurdistanê, hêz û aramiya Iraqê ye. author: Brian Hioe
title: Shen Reaches Across Political Aisle, Chiang Hits Out at Solar Panels in Second Mayoral Policy Presentation
content:
THE SECOND and last Taipei mayoral policy presentation was held on Saturday, November 21st. The major candidates are Puma Shen of the DPP and Chiang Wan-an of the KMT. Though a number of fringe candidates also presented, this article will focus on Shen and Chiang. The policy presentation was not a formal debate, in that there were no opportunities provided for candidates to question each other. Though the Shen campaign had pressed for further debates beyond the one formal debate that has taken place to date, the Chiang campaign is thought to be more reluctant.

Shen was the first to go. Shen first began by stressing bipartisanship, mentioning how Huang Shan-shan of the TPP had gifted him two signed copies of her book. To this extent, Shen raised how he hoped to learn from the experiences of past Taipei mayors, regardless of political affiliation. Indeed, non-partisanship has been something that Shen has been at odds to emphasize in past days, as a DPP candidate running in traditionally blue Taipei.

Shen proved more combative than in other debates or policy presentations, however. Shen criticized the Taipei city government for being insufficiently responsive to the public, as observed in its slow response to child abuse cases, a building collapse in Dazhi, and a food poisoning incident that killed six people in 2024. Shen also criticized the Chiang campaign for its unrealistic campaign pledges, such as relocating the Songshan Airport. At the same time, Shen continued to emphasize that his campaign had doubled down on positive campaigning, rather than a negative one that sought to take down political enemies, in framing them as hyperbolically bad.

Perhaps it was the fact that his campaign had emphasized negative campaigning to date that shaped Chiang’s response. Chiang’s policy presentation, then, primarily consisted of policy proposals and pledges. Chiang pledged a twenty-year plan for Taipei’s future development, including stimulating growth of the AI industry through the Shilin-Beitou Technology Park. In line with the KMT’s efforts to frame solar energy as dangerous, Chiang also reiterated a campaign pledge to remove solar panels at the Feitsui Reservoir.

To this extent, Chiang pledged to strengthen and further integrate transportation networks in Taipei, as well as to set up a new institute to research issues facing civil servants. Chiang also pledged to plant more trees in Taipei and expand the amount of greenery in the city. It proves of note that Chiang has made such a pledge, seeing as Puma Shen has doubled down on criticisms of the Taipei city government for reductions in the amount of greenery. In his policy presentation, Chiang mostly recited a long list of campaign pledges, taking advantage of his status as the incumbent

Chiang has increasingly leaned into framing Shen as a radical on cross-strait issues, while raising the possibility of a DPP victory provoking China in his campaign rallies. This occurs despite the fact that local elections are primarily about local issues, rather than cross-strait issues, and may occur because of desperation. It is of note, then, that he avoided such attacks in the debate, perhaps having gone too far in the direction of negative attacks on Shen.

It is probable that the policy presentation debate will not have much of an impact on voting, with little new that was exchanged between the two candidates, and relatively few differences from the first policy presentation. Shen leaned more into criticisms of Chiang that he had previously avoided, with Chiang having refused to engage in further debates because of the probable view that he would come off worse in a debate–indeed, Shen is known for his debating and public speaking skills, while Chiang has acquired a reputation as a relatively stiff and wooden speaker.

Still, one notes that Shen began both the first and second Taipei mayoral policy presentations with efforts to reach across the political aisle. This is telling about how his campaign hopes to win in historically blue-leaning Taipei.

author: Dulce Amor Rodriguez
title: Women seek justice for Duterte drug war victims
content:
Photo by Jonathan Sta. Rosa/NCCP

Trigger warning: details of violence and death

Seeing her son crying as she was about to leave for the market, she gave him a piece of candy. She later found him dead upon coming back home.

Emily Soriano was among the women whose loved ones were killed during former president Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war. They shared their accounts of the killings, highlighting their continuing struggle for justice with leaders of the World Council of Churches (WCC).

Members of Rise Up for Life and for Rights, a network of relatives of people killed during the anti-drug campaign, recounted their experiences during a dialogue organized by the National Council of Churches in the Philippines (NCCP).

The dialogue formed part of Thursdays in Black, a WCC campaign that seeks to end violence against women.

Aside from Soriano, Normita Lopez recounted how police shot her son despite his attempt to surrender. According to her, witnesses saw him raise both hands and plead with the police not to shoot but an officer pushed him down and shot him four times in the body and once in his right hand.

For her part, Jane Lee said that people ignored their pleas for justice before the WCC facilitated her travel to bring the families’ stories to the United Nations.

Estrella Nonay said, “I didn’t know how to get justice, so I joined Rise Up because I believe that if one of us gets justice, it is also justice for my son.”

“We are sharing with you sacred stories. Now that you have heard them, you are witnesses. We invite the WCC to stand in solidarity with the families of the victims in their quest for justice,” Deaconess Norma Dollaga of Rise Up said.

Rev. Merlyn Hyde Riley, vice-moderator of the WCC Central Committee, said that the testimonies exposed deeper structural, political, economic, social, and spiritual issues behind the killings. “No human being deserves to be treated in the ways you have described your loved ones having been treated,” Hyde Riley said.

Rev. Dr. Karen Georgia Thompson, general minister and president of the United Church of Christ and president of the World Communion of Reformed Churches, also called on churches to confront state violence against poor and marginalized communities.

She said that poor and marginalized communities bear the brunt of programs designed to harm them and urged churches to uphold human rights and dignity. (DAA)

author: Danilo Arao
title: Pagbabalik-tanaw
content:
Kayang kaya dahil kakayanin. May tagumpay dahil babakahin.

Sa nalalapit na pagtatapos ng 2026, mainam na balikan ang kalendaryong hindi na mabasa sa sobrang daming nakasulat.

Mula Enero hanggang Nobyembre, punong-puno ang iskedyul ng mga responsibilidad na kahit paano’y hinarap naman. Kahit ang susunod na buwan ng Disyembre, may mangilan-ngilan ding nakasulat kahit nakatakda itong panahon ng limitado pahinga. Opo, kailangan nang umupo’t humiga nang medyo matagal ang nakatatanda!

Kababalik lang mula sa sabbatical noong 2025, muling nagturo sa Unibersidad ng Pilipinas (UP) Diliman ngayong taon. Mas mataas na ang kumpiyansa sa gawaing pang-akademiko sa dalawang dahilan.

Una, natapos na ang doktoral na pag-aaral sa Alemanya noong 2024. Ikalawa, tumaas na ang posisyon at naging ganap na propesor (full professor) noong 2025, matapos ang 11 taon bilang kawaksing propesor (associate professor) at 11 pang taon bilang katuwang na propesor (assistant professor).

Sa wakas, nakamit din ang pang-akademikong “tagumpay” dahil sa tatlong letrang P, H at D na puwede nang ilagay sa dulo ng pangalan (at siyempre’y puwede na ring gamitin ang salitang “Doktor” kahit na hindi naman nagrereseta!).

Nagresulta ang bagong titulo’t ranggo sa mga bagong oportunidad. Matapos na maging ganap na kasapi (regular member) ng National Research Council of the Philippines (NRCP) noong Marso 2026, nakuha ang prestihiyosong NRCP Gabay Award para sa pananaliksik na may malaking pakinabang sa paghuhubog ng polisiya ng gobyerno.

Sa partikular, ito ay pagkilala sa ginawa ng Kontra Daya sa pagbubuo ng data set ng mga grupong partylist na tumakbo sa halalan noong 2025. Kahit na bagong miyembro pa lang, sinubukang magsumite ng dokumentasyon, lalo na ang paggamit ng iba’t ibang sangay ng gobyerno sa ginawang pananaliksik ng Kontra Daya, at pinalad namang kilalanin ng mga eksperto’t hurado ang kolektibong pinaghirapan ng grupo.

Sa mismong unibersidad, may ilang awards at grants na inaplayan at pinalad ring maaprubahan lahat. Sadyang nakakagulat ang 100% na approval rate pero nangyari talaga ito. Nagkaroon tuloy ng limitadong pondo para sa patuloy na pagtuturo, pananaliksik at gawaing ekstensiyon. Sa kabila ng patuloy na pagtaas ng presyo ng mga bilihin, nakayang bilhin ang mga kinakailangang gamit ngayong taon.

Dahil dito, mas maganda na ang kinakalabasan ng mga online na interbyu, pati na rin ang mga online na lektyur at talumpati sa loob at labas ng bansa. Pabirong hirit ng ilang kaibigan, kasama yata sa gastusin ang pagpaparetoke. Hindi po. Ilaw at kamera lang ang katapat ng bagong hilamos na mukha. (Huwag nang pag-usapan ang ilan pang bagong biniling gamit, salamat sa awards at grants.)

Sa taong ito, lumabas din ang tatlong librong inedit para sa isang dayuhang pabliser. Medyo mahal ito kung ibebenta sa mga kakilala sa Pilipinas kaya ginamit na lang ang bahagi ng pondo ng awards at grants para bilhin ang ilang kopya nito at ipamigay sa silid-aklatan ng mga piling unibersidad.

Kaya ngayon, libre itong mababasa ng maraming estudyanteng may panahong magpunta sa silid-aklatan. Nakakaintindi naman sila ng wikang Ingles kaya hindi malaking problema ang pagbabasa.

Pero kung nais ng nakasulat sa wikang Filipino, tinatayang lalabas sa Disyembre (sana lang!) ang ikapitong libro ng mga sanaysay. Matapos ang medyo mahabang panahon ng malalimang ebalwasyon at teknikal na pinalisasyon, mahahawakan na sa kamay ang ilang taong pinaghirapang buuin.

Kumpara sa mga naunang anim na libro, espesyal ang paparating na libro dahil tumulong ang mismong anak sa lettering ng pabalat ng libro. Siya rin ang gumawa ng ilustrasyon ng mga kabanata.

Sa madaling salita, awtor ang ama samantalang ilustrador ang anak. Siyempre’y may susing papel din ang asawang tinulungan ang anak sa gawain, bukod pa sa maraming suhestiyong parating sinusunod ng asawa sa usaping libro at buhay (o pabirong sabi sa wikang Ingles, “Yesband”).

Malapit nang matapos ang taong 2026. Nababawasan na ang mga nakasulat sa kalendaryo. Panahon nang maghabol para matapos ang kailangang matapos. Inaasahan ang limitadong pahinga sa mga natitira pang araw.

Kayang-kaya dahil kakayanin. May tagumpay dahil babakahin.

author: rti_admin
title: Class Interests in Casteless Disguise: Can Caste Be Disowned Without Surrendering Property and Lineage?
content:
‘I don’t believe in caste. I have no caste. Let’s build a casteless society.’ One hears this all the time now, from people who call themselves progressive, rationalist, liberal. On the face of it, there’s nothing to argue with. Who could object to that?

But look at the Indian socio-economic structure honestly, and the slogan starts to look less like idealism and more like a sleight of hand. Because you can’t abandon caste in your speech while quietly holding on to the wealth and advantages caste handed you. That isn’t annihilation of caste. It’s a way of protecting the hierarchy while pretending to be above it.

Louis Althusser, in Ideology and Ideological State Apparatuses (1970), made a point worth taking seriously here: ideology always exists in an apparatus, in practices—its existence is material. Caste is no different. It isn’t just a mental delusion people can shrug off. It has a material life, and in India that life runs through what we might call PPP: Property, Parents, Privileges.

Property means land, urban real estate, commercial capital—concentrated over generations in dominant-caste hands. Parents means lineage: hereditary prestige, ancestral standing, social capital kept carefully inside kin groups through endogamous marriage. Privileges means the leverage that comes from all of it—the networks that open doors in elite schools, boardrooms, professions, and commerce.

So when someone says they’ve “given up caste” because they dropped their surname, while still inheriting the family estate, the legacy networks, and the generational cultural capital—what exactly have they given up? You cannot disown caste while safeguarding the material lineage and property that caste produced. The two don’t come apart that easily.

Ambedkar: Annihilating Caste Means Annihilating Class

Ambedkar saw this clearly in Annihilation of Caste (1936). The caste order, he insisted, is not some innocent functional division of labour: “The Caste System is not merely division of labour. It is also a division of labourers.”

To the socialists of his day who thought economic reorganization alone would dismantle caste, he put the question squarely: can you have economic reform without first reforming the social order? If that order is graded by caste, what guarantee is there that Indian proletarians—divided into watertight caste compartments—will ever combine against their exploiters?

And on the myth of individual merit, he was blunt: those who benefit from birth, education, family name, business connections, and inherited wealth will win the race. But that isn’t a selection of the able. It’s a selection of the privileged. For Ambedkar, annihilation of caste was never about nominal changes in personal conduct. It demanded structural equality across economic, educational, political, and material life. Keeping the assets inside dominant groups while claiming caste is abolished runs directly against everything he argued.

The Biography of the “General Category”

Sociologist Satish Deshpande, in “Caste and Castelessness: Towards a Biography of the ‘General Category'” (2013), gave this rhetoric its proper name. Upper castes, he showed, have systematically laundered historical caste capital into the secular language of “merit” and individual competence. They shed the overt markers of caste, settle comfortably into the constitutionally unmarked “General Category,” and reinvent themselves as casteless modern citizens.

The burden of caste then gets shifted entirely onto SC, ST, and OBC communities—who are caricatured as “casteist” or backward for invoking affirmative action. Constitutional certificates become a badge of sectarian identity, while upper-caste generational capital passes as unmarked merit. That’s the strategy of the General Category, and Deshpande names it for what it is.

Lately there have been petitions before high courts—Telangana, Madras—asking for a “No Caste / Casteless” column in census forms, school transfer certificates, state applications. These deserve a closer look, because they tend to come in two flavours.

One is misguided cluelessness: well-meaning but politically naive people, from oppressed or liberal backgrounds, who imagine that leaving a box blank on a form dissolves structural violence. It doesn’t.

The other is more deliberate: an upper-caste design to escape structural accountability. If caste disappears from the census and public records, surveys can no longer measure how land, corporate wealth, and …

author: Dae-Oup Chang
title: International Labour Solidarity from Below: Reflections on Inter-Asian Solidarity Building of Asia Monitor Resource Centre
content:
Since its establishment in 1976, the Asia Monitor Resource Centre (AMRC) has served as a regional hub for labour solidarity in Asia. This article reflects on the AMRC’s half-century journey towards building inter-Asian labour solidarity. It discusses not only what AMRC has achieved, but also what it has failed to achieve, why it has failed, and what these experiences might tell us about the future of inter-Asian labour solidarity. This is a personal reflection, drawing on my 23 years of involvement with the AMRC in various capacities: as a full-time activist, a member of the Board of Directors, a member of the Regional Council, and Chair of the Board of Directors.


International labour solidarity has long occupied a prominent place in the political imagination of labour movements. Almost every major trade union has declared its commitment to internationalism. However, there is a considerable distance between internationalism as a declared principle and internationalism as an actual process of movement building. Affiliation to international trade unions, participation in international conferences, and occasional solidarity campaigns do not necessarily generate lasting solidarity among workers across national borders.


This distinction between international solidarity as a dead principle and as a living practice was central to an experiment in building bottom-up inter-Asian labour solidarity in which I participated during the 2000s as an AMRC activist coordinating the Asian Transnational Corporation Monitoring Network (ATNC Network). As  one of the regional labour networks AMRC initiated, the ATNC network sought to connect grassroots workers’ organisations across Asia. Its broader ambition was to build an alternative foundation for international labour solidarity in Asia. 


Building a Network from Below


When I joined AMRC in 2003, the ATNC Network already existed as a pilot initiative, with a substantial emphasis on

corporate codes of conduct

. Such an approach was becoming increasingly popular in international labour advocacy, particularly following the emergence of consumer campaigns targeting major international brands during the late 1990s and early 2000s.

1


We were sceptical of the political consequences of this prevailing model of north–south labour solidarity. Our scepticism concerned the underlying structure of solidarity that this approach

reproduced

. Northern organisations possessed the resources, connections, and influence required to pressure major brands, while workers and their organisations in Asian production sites were primarily positioned as

recipients of assistance

. The political focus often shifted from workers’ collective struggles to consumer organisations’strategies and their relationships with corporations.


Such campaigns sometimes achieved meaningful results. They can generate international attention, provide protection to workers, and force employers to negotiate. We did not deny their practical value. However, they had little to do with building the larger collective power of workers. For us, workers’ power was something to be built collectively by workers in and beyond workplaces rather than granted by individual employers’ moral behaviour. 


Therefore, we sought to reverse the direction of the network’s activities. Instead of beginning with corporations and their codes of conduct, we wanted to begin with workers’ struggles, their own organisations emerging from such struggles, and solidarity-based relationships built  between such organisations. 


These relationships developed through practical engagement. A group of workers or worker organisations might initiate a strike or an organising campaign. AMRC and its local partners could support the struggles on the ground. Over time, this process allowed us to include more organisations, whether unions or NGOs. Through such activities, new relationships emerged between organisations participating in the same struggles.

author: John David Parol
title: Trump Out, dumagundong sa Maynila sa kulminasyon ng protesta
content:
Sinalubong ng military honors ni Ferdinand Marcos Jr. si US President Donald Trump sa Malacañang kaninang umaga, Nobyemre 18, para sa kanilang bilateral meeting.

​Sa kabilang banda, kilometro lang ang layo mula sa palasyo, dumagundong ang panawagan ng sambayanan sa kulminasyon ng apat na araw na protesta kontra sa Pax Silica at sa imperyalistang Estados Unidos.

​Taliwas sa mainit na pagtanggap sa loob ng Malacañang, dahas at harang ang sumalubong sa mga nagpoprotesta sa lansangan.

Sa kahabaan pa lang ng Recto Avenue, hinarang na ang hanay ng mga raliyista at hindi pinayagang makapagmartsa patungong Mendiola. Hinarang din ng mga pulis ang mga delegasyon ng Gitnang Luson at Timong Katagalugan na nagmantini sa kampuhan sa Liwasang Bonifacio.

Hindi na napigilan ng galit na bulto ang magbulalas ng “Pax you, Trump” kasabay ng panawagang itigil ang Pax Silica at Trump Out.

Noong Nobyembre 17, pinuri ni Trump si Marcos Jr. sa pagsasabing mayroon itong “very good genetics” sa kanyang talumpati sa hapunan para sa mga lider ng ASEAN at Estados Unidos sa Maynila. Inalala rin ni Trump ang matagal na niyang pagkakakilala sa mga magulang ni Marcos Jr. bago pa siya naging pangulo ng Estados Unidos.

Para sa mga progresibong grupo, tumatagos sa katotohanan ang papuring ito, ngunit hindi bilang karangalan, kundi bilang patunay na manang-mana si Marcos Jr. sa kanyang ama at ina bilang masugid na papet ng Estados Unidos.

Hindi lingid sa kaalaman ng nakararami ang pagpapatayo ni Imelda Marcos ng mga pader upang itago ang kahirapan ng mga maralita noong idinaos ang Miss Universe sa bansa noong 1974. Sa kasalukuyan, gumastos ng humigit-kumulang ₱22.9 bilyon ang administrasyong Marcos Jr. kaugnay sa 49th ASEAN Summit. Ayon sa Defend Jobs Philippines, libo-libong maliliit na manininda at manggagawa ang pinatigil sa paghahanapbuhay sa tabing ng paglilinis sa daraanan ng mga dayuhang lider.

Sa isinagawang program sa Recto Ave., binatikos ni Bayan Secretary-General Raymond Palatino ang pag-host ni Marcos Jr. ng kauna-unahang leader-level QUAD meeting sa Pilipinas kahit hindi naman miyembro ng nasabing alyansang militar ang bansa.

Aniya, manang-mana rin si Marcos Jr. sa diktadurya ng kanyang ama sa paggamit ng makinarya ng estado at kapulisan upang supilin ang lehitimong pagkilos ng taumbayan.

Bago pa man buksan ang ASEAN summit, tatlong kabataang estudyante na ang inaresto sa University of Makati na lumahok sa ikinasang kilos-proteta laban sa Pax Silica noong Nobyembre 13. Habang may higit 200 indibidwal ang marahas na dinampot sa malawakang pag-aresto sa Muntinlupa at Kamaynilaan noong Nobyemre 15. Dagdag pa rito ang sa marahas na pagharang, panggigipit, paniniktik at iba pang porma ng brutalidad na ipinatupad ng Philippine National Police.

Inihalintulad naman ng National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers (NUPL) sa kalagayan noong Martial Law at pagkakaroon ng concentration camps noong World War II ang pagtrato sa mahigit 200 indibidwal na inaresto sa kasagsagan ng mga protesta kaugnay ng 49th ASEAN Summit.

“Ang pagtrato sa kanila bilang mga detinido ay hindi nalalayo sa pagtrato ni Marcos Sr. sa mga protesters noong Martial Law at pagtrato ni Hitler sa mga Hudyo noong World War II,” ani Atty. Arman Hernando ng Pro-Labor Legal Assistance Center (PLACE), isa sa mga abogadong tumayong legal counsel ng mga inaresto sa Muntinlupa.

Nanawagan ang NUPL sa agarang pagpapalaya sa lahat ng inaresto at pagpapanagot sa Philippine National Police (PNP), Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), at administrasyong Marcos Jr. sa paghahasik ng dahas at brutalidad laban sa mga aktibista.

​Wala mang 24 oras ang itinagal ng pagbisita ni Trump sa bansa, babala ng mga grupo na habambuhay namang pasanin ng sambayanang Pilipino ang epekto ng anumang hindi pantay na kasunduan o lihim na napag-usapan sa bilateral meeting nina Marcos Jr. at Trump.

Sa kabila ng maagang pahayag nina Marcos Jr. at Trump sa harap ng media na hindi muna pipirmahan ang Pax Silica sa biyaheng ito, bigla namang ibinida ni Trump sa state luncheon sa Malacañang na nakapagkasundo na sila sa tinawag niyang “very big trade deal—the biggest trade deal we’ve ever made by far.”

Nagsara naman ang programa sa Mendiola sa pamamagitan ng simbolikong pagsunog sa watawat ng Estados Unidos habang dumadagundong sa mga sound system ang kantang “Trump Out” ng Switchbitch na sinabayan ng sigaw at indak ng bulto.

Sa kulminasyon ng apat na araw na kilos-protesta, iginiit ng mga progresibong …

author: Lindsay McCabe
title: Changes to coronial legislation to broaden next-of-kin determinations
content:
Readers please be advised that this article mentions First Nations people who have passed away, including children.


On Tuesday 22nd September 2026, the Minns Labor Government announced changes to the

Coroners Act 2009

 NSW, specifically, the section of the legislation that instructs coroners to determine and appoint a Senior Next-of-Kin. This followed a statutory review of the Act, and is in response to one of the many recommendations made by the review. 


When a person’s death is reported to the coroner, a Senior Next-of-Kin is appointed. The Senior Next-of-Kin has the exclusive authority to make decisions regarding the person who has died while they are in the care of the coroner. For example, the Senior Next-of-Kin can object to a post-mortem examination being conducted. Being appointed Senior Next-of-Kin also means that the coroner has an obligation to provide mandatory notifications about the progress of a coronial investigation to the Senior Next-of-Kin. When, where and how a person is laid to rest is also under the authority of the Senior Next-of-Kin. 


Who is appointed as Senior Next-of-Kin is decided by a strict legal framework. The

Coroners Act 2009

 (NSW) s 6A states that the Senior Next-of-Kin must be the deceased person’s spouse or de facto partner; if they have no spouse or de facto partner, then any of the adult children of the deceased person can be appointed. If the person has no adult children, then the person’s parent/s may be appointed. 


This appointment-flow hierarchy has been problematic for Mob for many years, across many jurisdictions. It does not take into account our kinship systems, laws, or spiritual beliefs. One of the earliest challenges of the Senior Next-of-Kin hierarchy involved

two Aboriginal parents

 who could not agree on where to bury their deceased adult child. The mother wanted to hold a Catholic ceremony and burial in Darwin; the father however wanted to have a burial on their homelands, Bardi Country, and provided the Court with supporting information outlining the cultural obligations to do so. The Court ruled in favour of the mother. 


In

2016

, the NSW Supreme Court was asked to rule on a matter where the Senior Next-of-Kin appointment had been challenged. In this matter, the coroner had appointed a deceased man’s de facto partner as the Senior Next-of-Kin, as per the legislation. This allowed the partner, a Gumbaynggirr woman, to make arrangements for the deceased man’s burial to take place in Bowraville. The man’s sister however, wanted the man to be taken home to Weilwan Country and to be buried alongside his ancestors. The Court ruled in favour of the man’s de facto partner, citing common law precedent. Further, because the de facto partner of the deceased man established her de facto status to the Court, she held ‘administrative priority’; in other words, she had the highest right as per the legislation. 


More recently, in 2024, the Supreme Court of NSW decided on a dispute between a deceased man’s de facto partner and mother who could not agree on where to bury him. The de facto partner of the man insisted he wanted to be buried in La Parouse; his mother wanted to take him home to his father in Cherbourg, Wakka Wakka Country, where he could be buried on Country. The Court held in favour of the man’s de facto partner, accepting that she was the deceased man’s de facto partner at the time of his death. 


So, who is appointed Senior Next-of-Kin when a person dies has significant ramifications for where, when, and how a person is returned to Country. 


There have however been instances where the appointment of Senior Next-of-Kin has affirmed cultural responsibilities and laws, albeit outside of NSW. In

1999

, the non-Aboriginal spouse of a deceased Aboriginal man sought to bury them in Port Augusta. The deceased man’s father wished to bury him in Oodnadatta, where other members of the family had been buried, and on Yankintatjara Country. Several affidavits were presented to the Court, highlighting that, according to cultural responsibilities and practices, the head of the family should be empowered to make these decisions, not the spouse. The deceased’s spouse, on the other hand, argued that the children of the deceased would not be able to visit their father’s grave if it were located 700kms away in Oodnadatta. Significantly, the Court ruled in favour of the father of the deceased man, allowing him to take his son home, and to be buried according to …

author: Bizzi Lavelle
title: Young Women, Pain, Mobility Aids
content:
Stories Contributors Pitch an Idea

To be sick, or have a health condition of any kind is not a moral failing. I know this and I hope that you do too. However, every time I find myself staying in or leaving something early because I’m in pain or I’m fatigued, I can’t help but feel the people around me are disappointed.

People wish they had a friend who could come to their fortnightly event like they said they would. They wish they could book a performer to MC an event without them withdrawing due to spending that week pain ridden in bed. They wish the friend they extended a birthday party invite made it instead of sending through an apologetic message. They wish their friend would be in the room cheering them on at their weekly drag comp or production show.

A common online talking point echoes in my head as I send my latest “I’m sorry” message; you have to inconvenience yourself a little for the sake of your community. You have to be someone’s villager if you want to have a village.

With the weeks or days I spend hidden away, inside, barely leaving the house I often ask myself, do I deserve to be in anyone’s village? Do I deserve my own villagers?

The words to Rina Sawayama’s ‘Bad Friend’ circle my mind as I spend another Saturday night in my pajamas, watching anime in bed: “So don’t ask me where I’ve been, been avoiding everything.”

As I’m lamenting my woes to my notes app and the friends who get it, an article from The Times UK comes across my feed. “Why are young women using walking sticks?” by Katherine Stock. And then another, this time from The Telegraph, “How having a disability became cool” by Poppy Coburn.

The themes of these pieces are misogyny and ableism, with sprinkles of transphobia and ageism.

In both of these pieces, the authors seem to believe that young women in increasing numbers are faking to be disabled for social clout. In the first piece, Stock declares young women using mobility aids and posting about being ill are victims of “social contagion” deems the pain they’re in as “unclear” and therefore “unclear” if these women “really have” disabilities.

It’s wild to me, that in 2026, anyone would partake in such ableist vitriol. Despite what both authors think, there are a wide range of ways to be disabled. Disability and chronic illness don’t always look like a wheelchair user. Sometimes disabilities and chronic illnesses are invisible. Sometimes they’re dynamic. The only criteria to being disabled is having a condition, injury or alike that impedes you and your ability to do day to day tasks.

Disability is the only minority group a person can become part of at a moment’s notice, and is the only minority group we will all be part of at some point in our lives. As my friend, Protect our NDIS rally organiser and activist Oriela says “You will become disabled. That’s a promise not just a threat”.

That one influencer you follow could one day be surfing and the next using a wheelchair or cane. You aren’t able to discern how much pain someone is in by simply looking at them. If that were the case, women wouldn’t be waiting years for their pain to be believed and diagnosed.

For Aboriginal women, seeking medical care has an extra layer of stress. Racial bias in medicine historically saw beliefs that bla(c)k people, particularly women, have a higher pain tolerance than their white counterparts. This, along with classic medical misogyny has led to Aboriginal women being mistreated, ignored or treated as though they’re only ‘drug seeking’.

In Allanah Hunt’s 2024 piece ‘The Good Patient’, she details her experiences of medical racism as she navigates dealing with endometriosis. Despite Allanah’s attempts to present to hospitals as the best and most polite patient, her pain was still disbelieved and she was still treated as a drug seeker. “Because the truth is, no matter how much I’m ‘the good patient’, I will never escape the racial judgement from healthcare providers” Allanah writes.

Similarly, Colleen Lavelle (my mother) discusses her experience of medical racism in her 2017 piece. “Death by racism: bigotry in the health system is harming Indigenous patients’”.

She notes from her own experiences and other First Nations people whose medical experiences she’s listened to that a common thread is wondering if you’ve been overly sensitive.

One memory I have from my teens is when I was at the shops with my mum and younger sister. I went out to the car to put some bags in the car and a man …

author: Rudi Hartono, Peter Boyle
title: ‘Rising authoritarianism and militarism’ in Indonesia under Prabowo
content:
As the Indonesian economy sinks deeper into crisis, President Prabowo Subianto's government is becoming more authoritarian. Peter Boyle spoke to Rudi Hartono, one of the founding editors of the progressive publication Merdika.id about the current political situation. Hartono, a former editor of Berdikari Online left the People’s Democratic Party (PRD) because it moved to the right.

Recent events in Indonesia — the deployment of thousands of soldiers and tanks in Jakarta following reports of electronic surveillance [wiretapping] targeting President Prabowo Subianto and other government officials and the police raid on Gadjah Mada University — are reminiscent of the Suharto dictatorship’s New Order regime. Is a new and dangerous situation developing? If so, what lies behind it?

Yes, we are witnessing clear symptoms of rising authoritarianism and militarism. Although many had predicted this trajectory since Prabowo’s election victory, the speed and intensity of the process have been striking.

Since June 2026, the military has once again been deployed to confront protests — a move that evokes memories of the New Order. Large-scale troop mobilisations occurred during the demonstrations on October 20 (marking two years of the Prabowo-Gibran administration) and October 28 (Youth Pledge Day).

On one of those days, I received a WhatsApp message containing a video of tanks and marching soldiers on the streets, accompanied by the caption: “Thank your friends [referring to former PRD members who now support Prabowo and hold positions in government] for bringing the military back onto the streets.”

Yet the presence of soldiers on the streets only completes the picture of authoritarian consolidation that has taken shape over the past two years under Prabowo-Gibran.

Today, the 1998 reformasi has become little more than an artifact. Political power is once again concentrated in the executive (the presidency).

Many of the president’s remarks in speeches have quickly turned into policy — such as the roof-tile standardisation program or foreign-language lessons. The House of Representatives (DPR) has been reduced to a chorus, much like under the New Order.

There is no genuine opposition in the DPR. Even the Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle (PDIP), which remains outside the ruling coalition, has tended to be permissive toward the deteriorating situation.

The judiciary has suffered a similar fate: it is filled with government-aligned figures. The mechanisms of checks and balances have effectively disappeared.

It is not only the legislative and judicial branches that have been subdued. We are also seeing a process of recentralisation that is stripping regional and local governments of authority, fiscal resources, and responsibilities. Regional autonomy — one of the key achievements of the 1998 reform — is now little more than a skeleton being dragged toward its grave.

At the same time, freedom of expression is being heavily repressed. Paid "buzzers" [opinion-shapers] are deployed to drown out public criticism on social media, while the Ministry of Communication and Digital Affairs actively removes critical content. Cases of threats, intimidation, and doxxing against citizens in digital spaces are common. Mainstream media have adopted self-censorship. Under former President Joko Widowo (Jokowi), certain individuals monitored the media from the outside; under Prabowo, his people have entered the newsrooms themselves to supervise from within.

The presidential wiretapping issue, which provided the pretext for mobilising more than 20,000 troops and tanks on Jakarta’s streets, cannot be read simply as a clash between two elite factions. It more closely resembles the autogolpe [“self-coup”] schemes frequently seen in Latin America.

In my view, the issue was manufactured to serve three purposes at once. First, it supplied a justification for deploying more soldiers onto the streets. Second, it diverted public attention from structural problems — economic crisis, corruption, militarism, and others — toward a security narrative. Third, it was a crude tactic to redirect vertical public anger at the regime into a drama of elite infighting.

Before the wiretapping story surfaced, the regime was already under pressure from multiple fronts: forest fires in Kalimantan, Sumatra, and Papua; mass food poisoning from the free nutritious meal program (MBG) that has affected more than 50,000 children; the militarisation and expanding role …

author: Owen Marsden-Readford
title: The irrationality of the AI bubble is the irrationality of the market
content:
The AI investment boom is one of the largest bets in the history of capitalism. Money is pouring into the tech industry. Global AI spending is forecast to reach $2.7 trillion this year and $10 trillion cumulatively by 2032. The priorities of the system are obscene. Ending world hunger, according to the United Nations World Food Programme, would cost $40 billion per year. Amazon is spending over four times this on AI infrastructure this year.

In Australia alone, $150 billion is committed to building AI infrastructure over the next five years. That money could be life-changing for workers if it was used for almost anything else. Diverting the money from the data centre buildout could fund Australia’s health and Medicare budget for one year. Imagine the improvements we could make to an over-stretched and under-funded hospital system. With $150 billion, we could house the 200,000 households on the public housing waiting list at an average cost of just under half a million dollars and still have $50 billion left over. 

The $150 billion committed to data centres could also be used to pay for the Labor government’s aged care expansion package 38 times over. Or we could fund a significant chunk of the green transition needed to limit runaway climate change. The Australian Energy Market Operator places the cost of decarbonising the National Electricity Market by 2050 at $122 billion.

​Alas, the ever-rational invisible hand of the market has decided that we need more data centres to power Elon Musk’s Grok AI and its

 epic, vulgar roasts

.

​That the AI boom is socially destructive is irrelevant to investors. Data centres guzzle fossil fuels and water and are a significant source of noise pollution, emitting a constant low, droning hum. Most of the data centre buildout is happening in working-class and poorer communities in Western Sydney, not in Mosman or Toorak.

In recent weeks, the AI stock market boom has faced a sharp downturn. This is not because the world’s capitalists have taken notice of the socially and environmentally destructive nature of the industry, but because they are concerned that future windfall profits may not materialise.

​AI is now integrated into the militaries across the world, the result of an AI arms race. The results are terrifying. Take Russia’s

 

ZALA Lancet drone

, which uses AI to spot and dive bomb targets free from human oversight.

​Bosses are using AI as an excuse to sack workers. In the past few weeks alone, Qantas, NAB and Canva have announced over 4,000 redundancies cumulatively. Moreover, the data centre buildout is pushing inflation upwards, which the Reserve Bank is using as an excuse to raise interest rates, pushing unemployment higher. It is yet another way the AI boom is coming at the expense of the working class.

​The insanities of the AI boom are the insanities of the market. It is only in a capitalist society driven by profit and competition that it makes sense for trillions of dollars to be ploughed into AI while working-class needs are neglected. For anything that would benefit the working class, governments and capitalists across the world cry poor. Yet when there’s a share market boom, trillions find their way into it with no thought for what society actually needs. 

It’s not like people are crying out for data centres. In the US midterm elections, when data centres were on the ballot, voters rejected data centre expansion or approved local restrictions in 40 out of 41 ballot measures. AI data centres are unpopular yet continue to be imposed on ordinary people. Genuine democracy and the capitalist market are incompatible.

Under capitalism, production occurs to enrich the capitalist class, not to meet human needs. Karl Marx wrote in Capital: “Accumulate, accumulate! That is Moses and the prophets!” In a market economy, maximising shareholder value counts for more than the cries of hungry children or the plight of the homeless. 

​The AI boom is making many capitalists astronomically rich. Tech billionaires gained a combined $845 billion through the first nine months of this year. The stock market has reached record highs multiple times in 2026. The benefits of the AI bubble concentrate at the top, in the hands of corporate executives, financiers and the rich more generally. Workers, on the other hand, receive almost nothing. There is no boom in wages. Huge speculative wealth sits alongside stagnant or falling living standards.

​No boom, however, can last forever …

author: Stan Miller, Victor Osprey
title: France: ‘The leadership of the movement belongs to the students themselves’
content:
Stan Miller is a member of the French revolutionary socialist organisation Nouveau parti anticapitaliste — Révolutionnaires (New Anticapitalist Party — Revolutionary, NPA–R) in Montpellier. He spoke to Victor Osprey on November 9 about the youth uprising in France and the role being played by trade unions and the revolutionary left.

What were the immediate political results of the November 5 general strike called by French trade unions in response to cost-of-living pressures and public service cuts, which mobilised an estimated 1 million people or more?

Today [November 9], the prime minister [Sébastien Lecornu] met with union leaders for the first time in a while. This was a direct consequence of the mobilisation by high school students who strong-armed the unions to do anything. The prime minister said was willing to raise the minimum wage by 1.6 % (about €1502 a month), which is way below inflation.

There are eight national trade union confederations in France. Almost all local unions are affiliated to one of them. The politics of these eight confederations is shaped by history: for example, the CGT [Confédération Générale du Travail, General Confederation of Labour] used to be controlled by the Communist Party and was very strong in blue collar industries; the CFDT [Confédération française démocratique du travail, French Democratic Confederation of Labour] is more social democratic; the FSU [Fédération Syndicale Unitaire, United Trade Union Federation] almost exclusively covers teachers.

Some people divide them between “reformists” and “radicals”, but all defend the interests of their own bureaucracy rather than the interests of the movement. Some unions, such as the CFDT, say the wage hike is not high enough but believe the government is an honest partner and want to negotiate wages across different industries.

The CGT believes in negotiating but wants to convince the government that they cannot be ignored; that is why they have called a day of strikes and actions on November 17 to show off a bit of muscle. The CFDT has decided not to join the strike on November 17. The CGT called the November 5 strike just one month before, showing that they had no genuine desire to help the youth movement [which started in September], otherwise they would have called it sooner.

The spark for the general strike was the powerful movement of youth and students against the under-funding of the education system. Has it led to offers of further concessions from the French government, on top of previous offers given to youth and students? Is the government attempting to sideline the demands of organised workers and separate them from the students by appealing for “dialogue” with trade union leaders?

The prime minister invited youth organisations to discuss the future of education. Also present at the meeting was the far-right youth organisation UNI [Union Nationale Inter-universitaire, Inter-University Union] and several far-right MPs, so the left representatives walked out. We will not discuss anything in the presence of the far right.

There are several youth organisations and student unions, but participation in student elections is very low, generally only a few percent of students vote. They do not act as unions defending the immediate interests of students — though there are some exceptions at a very local level. Instead, they mainly act as political organisations defending a particular vision.

A few weeks ago, the education minister [Édouard Geffray] tried to calm the youth movement with scraps such as creating 15,000 additional higher education places. But youth organisations are asking for 260,000 new university spots.

The government is trying to divide workers and students, but many are not falling for it. Tomorrow [November 10] is a day of action and strike for both teachers and students.

How has the far-right Rassemblement national (National Rally, RN) reacted to the general strike and the movement overall?

This movement is polarising people. There are many instances of people reacting to police brutality against the youth. We have had almost as many police arrests of youth protesters in one month as we did in one year of Yellow Vest protests. But some workers are also saying the police should shoot the protesters.

Overall, it is a hard time for the far right because [President Emmanuel] Macron is kind of stealing their talking points: more police, more brutality, etc.

Can the movement effectively translate …

author: Simon Upitis
title: Protesters Shut Down Bisalloy Steels - Again
content:
Hundreds of protesters shut down Bisalloy Steels on Sunday 15 November, preventing it from operating for 48 hours. This was the eleventh time Wollongong Friends of Palestine (WFOP) had organised a picket of the company.

Bisalloy Steels produces armour plating used by the IDF and by West Bank settlers to oppress Palestinians. Steel plate produced by Bisalloy is used to retrofit civilian vehicles with armour plating, making them bulletproof and allowing them to be fitted with roof-mounted machine guns. Bisalloy is also set to benefit from Australia’s increased military spending via the AUKUS agreement. In July, Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy announced a $2 million contract would be awarded to Bisalloy to produce steel for US Virginia-class nuclear submarines. 

The picket had a lively atmosphere. A makeshift stage was set up at one entrance with DJs, live music and poetry readings. Free food and first aid were provided by volunteers. Dozens of activists camped overnight, ensuring that the company couldn't sneak workers through the picket in the early hours of the morning. Attendees came from far and wide, with many travelling down from Sydney. Palestine Action Bega Valley attended as a group. Other groups with an official presence included the NSW Socialists and the Illawarra Greens.

At the other entrance, political discussions were held in gazebos set up on the street, often involving dozens of attendees. One member of WFOP recently returned from the West Bank recounted their experiences defending Palestinian farms from settler violence. Nurses spoke against their regulatory agency’s adoption of a Zionist definition of antisemitism. There was debate about the type of movement required to free Palestine and the tactics and strategies needed to push the struggle forwards. NSW Socialists held a forum with the candidate for Wollongong in the state election, Ryan Chapman. The success of the various workshops and discussions prove the pickets can be a place for left-wing people to gather and discuss live political questions. 

This picket experienced much less police harassment and intimidation than the previous one. In June, the company planned to break through the picket line and bring a busload of workers into the site. We stopped them, but the police maintained a heavy presence on that occasion. One attendee was arrested. Another was violently thrown to the ground, and everyone else was subjected to their petty demands and often thuggish behaviour. Riot squad cops also came down from Sydney. 

This time, we heard on Sunday night that Bisalloy wouldn’t try to bring in workers until we left. Throughout the picket, there was a very minor police presence, normally a single cop car. This was a significant victory. It shows the company wasn’t confident enough to directly confront our community campaign.

Of course, we can’t be complacent. At some point, the company will get fed up with the disruptions and take a more combative and confrontational approach. In the meantime, the campaign remains committed to stopping Bisalloy profiting from genocide.

author: @ndy
title: The struggle is real with Jillian Segal.
content:
See also : Jillian Segal and husband funding far-right group “Advance”, Anthony Klan, The Klaxon, July 12, 2025.

Jillian Segal — the South African–born Australian lawyer, business executive, and Australia’s Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism — recently dropped another Report, ASECA Priorities. According to the Special Envoy, a newly-hatched “modern progressive antisemitism” … is taking “the hostility of Islamic extremism and far-left antisemitism, together with traditional antisemitic tropes”.

My first reaction on reading this passage was to recall the unforgettable 2014 framing by the Australian Defence League of the alleged “evil anarcho-pinko-anarchist-islamic cabal of dirt”; the wicked coalition then allegedly intent on turning Penrith into a no-go zone for patriots.

In any case, inre the Report, Jeffrey Loewenstein doesn’t hold back in It’s time to sack Jillian Segal (Deepcut News, November 2, 2026), the Jewish Council of Australia (October 30, 2026) has slammed it, and Jeff Sparrow has characterised it, not unfairly, as a Trumpian plan to curtail free speech (Crikey, November 2, 2026). The Report is also subject to critical scrutiny by Robert Manne, who examines it in On the Rise of Antisemitism in Australia (November 8, 2026), along with the thoughts of Lord Andrew Roberts and Sir Simon Schama on the subject of ‘antisemitism’. Manne concludes that:

Schama believes he can help combat the rise of antisemitism in the Diaspora by defending the indefensible, the war crimes of the IDF under Benjamin Netanyahu. I believe a more likely remedy would be for leading Diaspora thinkers, like Schama, and influential publishers, like Morry Schwartz, and the leaders in Australia of the principal Israel and Jewish lobbies, like Jillian Segal, to speak the truth about what, under Netanyahu and the two Kahanist-fascist members of his Government, Israel has become, and the moral revolution that has to happen in Israel if Jews in the Diaspora are to be spared from the dreadful rise of antisemitism that is spreading around the Western world.

FWIW, for over 20 years I’ve been attempting, inter alia, to monitor and document organised, public expressions of antisemitism and other racisms in Australia — the better to disrupt it. I’m also an anarchist, and one of many people to hold the view that the Israeli state has engaged in a genocidal assault upon Palestine in the three years since October 7 (the latest chapter in a much longer history of deadly state violence). On that basis, I assume that Segal et. al. would categorise myself as an exponent of ‘far-left antisemitism’, the meaning of which is elaborated upon in this passage:

Far-left antisemitism or issue-motivated antisemitism

Far-left ideology and associated activism feature a worldview that casts the world in terms of ‘oppressors’ and ‘oppressed’. Within this binary framework, Israel is portrayed as a colonial project that is inherently racist and Jews who support Israel’s existence are portrayed as representatives of ‘whiteness’ (regardless of their ethnicity), privilege (regardless of their means), imperialism (notwithstanding the absence of an empire), greedy capitalism and the projection of Western power.

This framing allows longstanding antisemitic motifs to be repackaged in the academic language of anti-racism, decolonisation, human rights, social justice and intersectionality, often in service of a traditional Marxist revolutionary agenda.

When a cause is believed – with ideological fervour – to be absolutely just, its ends can come to justify any means and its adherents can feel free to vilify, harass and seek to destroy those who associate with what is framed as evil.

Over time, the language of human rights and its greatest crimes – apartheid, ethnic cleansing, genocide, etc. – has increasingly been appropriated to portray Israel (and, relevantly, members of the Jewish community who support it) as morally evil, often to the point of being equated to Nazis.

In contemporary Australia, elements of Australia’s historically fringe radical left have sought to appeal to well-meaning mainstream progressive Australians who may perceive the Palestinian cause as a matter of social justice. This ‘gateway’ issue, of sorts, has been used by far-left activists to magnify their appeal and prominence and to attempt to introduce traditionally moderate Australians to radical and anti-Jewish propaganda that would previously have been of little interest.

author: Tony Smith
title: AI breeds homogeneity — the antithesis of folk music
content:
For unique and indigenous cultural forms to survive and evolve, they need to withstand the homogenisation of cultures that is part of the process of global capitalism. For some cultures, geographical isolation, and the continuation of traditional farming practices allowed this.

Folklorists describe how communities living in isolated valleys or mountainous areas often have customs very distinct from those of their neighbours, due to differences in terrain and mode of production.

This phenomenon manifests in variations of songs, dance tunes and airs that are unique to specific groups and geographical locations.

But the growth of capitalism encroached upon indigenous and traditional ways of life, with industrialisation forcing rural populations onto the cities, and with mining and agribusiness destroying traditional modes of farming.

New forms of transport meant geographical distances could now be covered in shorter times. Mass communication facilitated the sharing and exchange of unique cultural practices, but at the same time introduced the cultural practices of ruling elites which often dominated local traditions.

Sometimes debates arise about ‘correct’ or ‘original’ versions of traditional folk tunes and songs. These arguments might not seem to have great importance — but folk musicians instinctively fear that their unique cultural practices and way of life is being threatened.

Folk musicians are concerned about the motives of outsiders who record or listen to their music. This distrust can inhibit the work of folklorists who are studying and preserving a song or tune in good faith.

The movie Songcatcher (2000) tells the story of a musicologist who finds versions of lost traditional English songs like Barbara Allen and Moonshiner preserved in the remote Appalachian mountains in the United States. These songs are then recorded and repatriated.

But problems arise when one particular version of a song or tune is recorded — either in audio or in musical notation — because it advantages one version over others.

For genuine folklorists, a tune or song is organic and mutable. It is the nature of folk songs to vary according to the occasion, the influence of singers’ moods, and whether a singer feels in good voice. There is no bland setting into stone and this is part of the excitement of folk music.

Folk song collectors with integrity acknowledge multiple versions. On the Mainly Norfolk site for example, most songs are presented with at least two interpretations.

Folk singer Shirley Collins warns that commercialisation brings compromise. In her memoir All on the Downs, Collins explains that commercialisation means songs and singers lose integrity, and a sense of the genuine and the vital connection between songs and places.

A feature of folk music is the direct, oral transmission of songs and tunes. Considering her role in the tradition, Collins reckoned that when she sang, she felt generations of folk singers standing behind her, and became a “conduit for their songs, a link in a mysterious chain ... responsible for maintaining their integrity”.

Shirley Collins’ experiences should be compulsory reading for anyone interested in the preservation of folk traditions. When we hear folk music we easily imagine a specific landscape, its flora and fauna and its people. This is something that cannot be bought or imposed from outside. It touches our inner beings.

Paradoxically, one of the ways traditional music survives is that folkies (folk musicians) write new material. This is not only permissible but it is important for maintaining traditions. When folkies write new songs and tunes, they respect traditions and work within its broad bound.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) does not respect traditions but exploits them, mimicking them for commercial reasons. Difference is everything in the folk tradition. AI, however, smooths out wrinkles and obliterates individuality.

Consider Mick’s Misfortunes, a series of AI generated folk-style songs on YouTube. Ironically, most of Mick’s difficulties relate to aspects of his life forced upon him by technological changes. In these songs, the lyrics are fine, but the production is so uniform that it reduces everything to a bland mass.

Feeling the essence, rather than merely observing as an outsider is important in folk music. There is no evidence that AI understands sentiment.

APRA AMCOS (Australian Performing Rights Association / Australian Mechanical Copyright Owners Society) …

author: Unknown
title: Erkunt’ta satış sonrası işçileri ne bekliyor?
content:
Ankara— Erkunt Sanayi A.Ş., Sincan ve Etimesgut'taki fabrikaları ile nisan ayında Hisarlar Makina'ya satılmıştı. Eylül başında yönetim değişikliği tamamlanırken işçiler yeni yönetimden ücret ve çalışma koşullarının beklentisi içerisindeydi. Yeni yönetimle geçen iki ayın ardından Erkunt işçileri ile konuştuk.

Eski yönetime dair çeşitli iddia ve dedikoduların fabrikada yayıldığını anlatan bir döküm işçisi, ''Eski yönetimin mâli hesaplarında bir sürü usulsüzlük olduğuna dair dedikodular duyduk. Buna bizim banka promosyonlarımız da dahil. Yıllardır burada çalışıyorum. İlk defa son banka promosyonunda brüt maaşa endeksli yatırıldı. Kişi başı 100-150 bin TL gibi rakamlar konuşurken herkese 50-60 bin TL yattı. Eski personel müdürünün işine de son verilmiş, mahkemelik oldular diye duyduk eski yönetim için. Şimdi yeni yönetim bu hesapların hepsinin üstüne gidecekmiş. Bizim beklentimiz de öyle yapması. Bizim hakkımızı yiyen varsa cezasını alsın. Varsa haklarımızı versinler'' dedi. Görüştüğümüz başka işçiler de bu iddiaları duyduklarını söylüyor.

Yeni yönetimin Etimesgut'taki fabrikada işçilerin de katıldığı bir toplantı yaptığını aktaran işçiler, ''Ne şikayetiniz varsa söyleyin çözülecek” dediler. Şuan için malzeme eksikliklerinde bir sorun yok. Yemekhane koşulları, yemekler de çok iyileşti. Ancak Hisarlar'ı ilk satın aldıklarında işçilere ek zam verildiğini duyduk. Aynı beklenti bizde de var. Bizim beklentimiz çok ama esas sözleşmede göreceğiz ne kadar işçiyi düşündüklerini'' dediler.

Ek zamma dair somut bir gelişme yokken beyaz yakalı işçiler, kendi çift maaşlarının kesildiğini anlattılar: ''Bizim normalde çift maaş aldığımız aylar vardı. Yeni yönetim sizin eski yönetimle anlaşmanız bizi bağlamaz diyip kestirip attı. Telafi olarak da Ocak ayında fazladan zam yapacağız dediler ama ne kadar yaparlar, bizim çift maaş ikramiyelerini kurtarır mı bilmiyoruz. Biz açıkçası endişeliyiz. Ödeme planlarımızı buna göre ayarlamıştık. Şimdi ne olacak belli bile değil.''

Erkunt'un geçtiğimiz günlere kadar 3 farklı taşeron firma ile anlaşması vardı. Yeni yönetim, bunlardan en büyüğü ile anlaşmasını geçtiğimiz haftalarda sonlandırdı. İşine son verilen taşeron işçilerden kimileri kadroya alınırken kimileri işten çıkarıldı. Kadroya alınan işçilerin başlangıç ücreti de tartışmalara sebep oldu. Etimesgut döküm fabrikasından bir işçi, ''Ben 4 yıldır bu fabrikada çalışıyorum. 1-2 senedir taşeronda çalışanları 60 bin TL'den başlatmışlar diye duyduk. Benim kendi maaşım daha o kadar değil. Bize de iyileştirme yapmaları lazım'' derken, 6 ay önce işe başladığını söyleyen başka bir işçiyse ''Bana verdikleri para 43 bin TL. Ben 6 ay önce taşerondan işe girmiş olsam ve şuan kadroya alınsam en az 50 bin TL verirlerdi bana da. Bize de iyileştirme şart'' dedi.

Erkunt'taki son TİS sürecine işçiler ve yetkili Türk-Metal Sendika'sı arasındaki hararet damgasını vurmuştu. Sendikadan önce taslak hazırlamak için dijital platformları kullanan işçiler, kendi yaptıkları anketler ile taleplerini belirlemişti. Sendika kendi taslağını daha düşük ücret, yan hak zamları ile açıklamasına rağmen işçiler kendi hazırladıkları taslağa sahip çıkmıştı. Bunun için fabrikaya bildiriler dağıtıp, stickerlar yapıştırmış, fabrika önlerine pankartlar asmıştı. İşçiler, sendika temsilcilerini sık sık fabrika içinde sıkıştırırken işçiler ile sendika temsilcileri çeşitli tartışmalarda karşı karşıya gelmişti.

Tüm bunlardan sonra yapılan sendika delege seçimleri ise sessiz geçti. Süreci anlatan bir makine işçisi, ''Delege adayı listeleri asmışlar panolara. Seçim yapacağız diye duyurdular. Her şey çok hızlı gelişti. Sendika temsilcilerine kimler yakınsa onlar seçildi açıkçası'' derken Sincan'daki bir döküm işçisi, ''Bizim sendika temsilcimiz işten çıkarılmıştı. Bizim de başımıza bir anda birini diktiler yeni sendika temsilcisi bu diye. Seçim yok bir şey yok. Nasıl olacak bu iş?'' diye ifade etti.

Geçmiş dönemleri hatırlatan bir işçi, ''Bizim şuan ücretlerimiz diğer döküm fabrikalarına göre düşük. Yeni yönetim belki vergiyi yüzde 15 sabitler diye umuyordum ama ses seda yok. Biz önceki sözleşmeye dair ne yaptıysak aynısını yapmamız lazım. O zaman taleplerimizi belirlemiştik. Herkes arka çıkmıştı beraber hareket ediyorduk. Aynısını yapmadığımız sürece önümüzdeki sözleşme bizim açımızdan sıkıntılı geçer. Bizdeki sendika temsilcileri sırf yeni yönetime yaranmak için düşük taslak bile açıklayabilir. Çok değil Ocak'ta duyurmuş olurlar. Ne yapıyorsak öncesinde yapmamız lazım'' diyerek işçilerin …

author: Mag
title: „Linke ausrotten“: Der neue ultrarechte Präsident Abelardo de la Espriella ist eine Gefahr (nicht nur) für Menschenrechte und Friedenspolitik in Kolumbien
content:
Dossier


„

Eine Gruppe von 21 internationalen Menschenrechtsorganisationen, darunter das Internationale Büro für Menschenrechte in Kolumbien (Oidahco), warnt vor der bevorstehenden Politik des ultrarechten gewählten Präsidenten Abelardo de la Espriella. Sie befürchten einen möglichen Abbau von Menschenrechten, Rückschritte bei der Umsetzung des Friedensabkommens von 2016 und der Friedenspolitik sowie eine Aushöhlung der Rechte von Frauen und LGBTIQ+-Personen. (…) Sein „Sofortplan“ sieht vor, den Einflussbereich bewaffneter Gruppen durch weitläufige Militäroperationen in den ersten 90 Tagen seiner Regierung zurückzudrängen. (…) Die unterzeichnenden Menschenrechtsnetzwerke fordern die Europäische Union und ihre Mitgliedstaaten sowie die Schweiz, Norwegen und das Vereinigte Königreich daher auf, die künftige Regierung De la Espriellas zur Einhaltung der Verpflichtungen des kolumbianischen Staates aus dem Friedensabkommen von 2016 zu bewegen

…“

Artikel von Pablo Schröder vom 26.06.2026 in amerika21

 und mehr zum Thema:


Landesweiter Streik und große Mobilisierung am 19.November erzwangen einige Rückzieher in der geplanten Steuerreform der rechten Regierung Kolumbiens


Kolumbien: Steuerreform und Proteste der Bevölkerung


„

Eines der auffälligsten Merkmale dieser ersten 100 Tage der Amtszeit des „Showmans“ Abelardo ist die Improvisation seiner Regierung. Programmatisch gesehen ist es eine Regierung, die von der Uribisten-Rechten abhängig ist – einer neoliberalen Rechten, die Dogmen und Irrtümer vertritt, für die es heute weltweit kaum noch Befürworter gibt, die hier jedoch als Wundermittel für all unsere Übel angepriesen werden. (…)


Die Ankündigung des nationalen Streiks, zu dem unter anderem die Gewerkschaftszentrale „Central Unitaria de Trabajadores“, der „Pacto Histórico“, Bauern- und Indigenenorganisationen sowie der kolumbianische Lehrerverband aufgerufen hatten, zwang die Regierung dazu, bei einigen der rückschrittlichsten Punkte einen Rückzieher zu machen, und stellt einen vorweggenommenen Sieg der für heute geplanten Massenmobilisierung dar. Dennoch enthält der Entwurf der Steuerreform weiterhin Aspekte, die den einkommensschwächsten Bevölkerungsgruppen schaden, während Sektoren wie der Finanzsektor, der in Kolumbien geringer besteuert wird als Unternehmen – was nicht so sein sollte –, unberührt bleiben. Der Vorschlag enthält einige Abgaben, die erforderlich sind oder auf die man sich einigen kann und die bereits von der vorherigen Regierung dem Kongress vorgelegt, dort jedoch nicht verabschiedet wurden, wie zum Beispiel die Steuer auf Online-Glücksspiele, die Erhöhung der Kohlenstoffsteuer, die Steuer auf Gelegenheitsgewinne sowie die Erhöhung der Steuern auf Spirituosen, E-Zigaretten und Zigaretten. diese Steuern sowie die sogenannten Gesundheitssteuern sollten verabschiedet werden, denn es darf nicht außer Acht gelassen werden, dass eine Steuerreform erforderlich ist. (…)


Aus all diesen Gründen waren der landesweite Streik und der große Mobilisierungstag im ganzen Land ein riesiger Erfolg. Die Menschen sind nicht bereit, sich ihre Rechte nehmen zu lassen, wie es die Regierung beabsichtigt. Die Angst vor sozialen Unruhen hat zwar die negativsten Aspekte der Reform rückgängig gemacht, doch bestehen weiterhin ernsthafte Probleme hinsichtlich der verbleibenden Teile dieses Steuerreformvorhabens

.“ span.

Artikel von Pedro Santana Rodríguez vom 24. November 2026 in LoQueSomos

title: Comienza el juicio por el crimen de Cristian Pereyra, el docente asesinado por un policía mientras trabajaba para DiDi
content:
Este miércoles 25 de noviembre comenzará el juicio oral por el asesinato de Cristian Pereyra, docente que trabajaba como conductor de DiDi – como miles de trabajadores/as de la educación, que necesitan sumar otro ingreso para llegar a fin de mes – y que fue asesinado de cinco disparos por la espalda por el policía bonaerense Matías Vizgarra Riveros. El efectivo llega al debate detenido con prisión preventiva y acusado de homicidio criminis causa agravado por el uso de arma de fuego. Con al consigna «¡Basta de precarización laboral, basta de impunidad, justicia por Cristian!», su familia convoca a organismos de derechos humanos, organizaciones sociales, políticas y sindicales, docentes y a la comunidad a acompañar el inicio del debate, que se realizará desde las 9 en el Tribunal Oral en lo Criminal N°1 de San Justo. También reclama que se garantice la publicidad del juicio, cuya sala tiene capacidad para apenas 20 personas.

Por ANRed.


Este miércoles 25 de noviembre comenzará el juicio oral por el

asesinato de Cristian Pereyra

, un docente que debió trabajar como conductor de DiDi para complementar sus ingresos y llegar a fin de mes.

Fue asesinado de cinco disparos por la espalda por Matías Vizgarra Riveros, un efectivo de la Policía Bonaerense

. El debate se desarrollará

desde las 9 en el Tribunal Oral en lo Criminal N° 1

, ubicado en Mendoza 2417/23, segundo piso, en

San Justo

, partido de

La Matanza

.


Cristian era docente y la precarización laboral y los bajos salarios que perciben miles de trabajadores de la educación lo llevaron a buscar otro ingreso. Necesitaba renovar el alquiler de su vivienda y comenzó a trabajar con la aplicación DiDi. En ese contexto fue asesinado

. La familia reclama que el crimen sea juzgado con la máxima pena posible y que se considere la condición policial del acusado como un agravante.


La causa está caratulada como

homicidio criminis causa agravado por el uso de arma de fuego

 y Vizgarra Riveros permanece detenido con prisión preventiva. En el comunicado, la familia sostiene que la investigación reunió numerosas pruebas que lo vinculan con el crimen:

el pedido del viaje desde su propio teléfono celular, registros de antenas de telefonía que lo ubicarían en el lugar de los hechos, imágenes de cámaras de seguridad que lo identificarían conduciendo el vehículo y estacionándolo en el punto donde fue encontrado, además de registros de su ingreso a la UTOI con la misma ropa

. También menciona una

pericia balística positiva sobre los casquillos hallados en la escena

.


Entre los elementos incorporados a la investigación, la familia destaca la declaración de un superior policial que afirmó que Vizgarra Riveros le dijo

«me la mandé»

 y que, después de dispararle a Cristian, consultó a otro efectivo que prestaba servicio en el Hospital Simplemente Evita si había ingresado alguna persona herida de bala.

El acusado niega la autoría del crimen, pero la familia considera que las pruebas reunidas son contundentes y exige una condena

.


El comunicado también denuncia las maniobras de la defensa para limitar el acompañamiento público al juicio. Según informaron,

los abogados del acusado solicitaron que medios de comunicación, organizaciones sindicales y organismos de derechos humanos no pudieran acercarse a menos de 200 metros del tribunal. Ese planteo fue rechazado

. Sin embargo, la familia advierte que la publicidad del debate seguirá restringida:

la sala asignada tiene capacidad para apenas 20 personas

, pese a que se espera la presencia de cientos de personas y organizaciones.


Ante esa situación,

organismos de derechos humanos y SUTEBA La Matanza presentaron un

amicus curiae

 para solicitar que se garantice la publicidad del juicio

. Si bien no se consiguió una sala con capacidad acorde al interés social que despertó el caso, el tribunal informó que transmitirá los alegatos de apertura y cierre. La familia espera que también puedan seguirse de esa manera la lectura de la sentencia y sus fundamentos.


«

La defensa del acusado ataca a nuestra familia solo por hacer público nuestro reclamo de justicia; quieren coartar nuestra libertad de expresión y la de todos los que exigen justicia por Cristian»

, señala el comunicado. El reclamo pone en el centro no solo el asesinato de un trabajador, sino también las

condiciones de precarización que atraviesan quienes deben multiplicar sus jornadas laborales para sostener sus vidas y las de sus familias

.
