title: Aydın Ekmek ve Gül’den 25 Kasım Paneli: Kadınların mücadelesi ve dayanışması büyüyor
content:
Aydın Ekmek ve Gül grubu, 22 Kasım’da saat 14.00’te Milli Aydın Bankası’nda, 25 Kasım Kadına Şiddete Karşı Uluslararası Mücadele Günü öncesinde panel düzenledi. Panelde kadınlar; şiddete, cezasızlığa, eşitsizliğe ve sömürüye karşı bir araya geldi.

Panelin açılış konuşmasını Aydın Ekmek ve Gül’den Şükriye Karalar yaptı. Karalar, 25 Kasım Kadına Yönelik Şiddete Karşı Uluslararası Mücadele Günü’nün tarihsel önemine değinerek Mirabel Kardeşlerden bugüne miras kalan mücadeleyi anlattı. Kadınların yıllardır sürdürdüğü eşitlik, özgürlük ve yaşam hakkı mücadelesinin önemini vurguladı.

Kadınların yoğun katılım gösterdiği panelde Avukat İlgin Ceribaş ve Sosyal Hizmet Uzmanı Hilal Yılmaz konuşmacı olarak yer aldı.

Avukat İlgin Ceribaş, şüpheli kadın ölümleri üzerinden cezasızlık politikasını ele aldı. Kadın ölümlerinin aydınlatılması, sorumluların ortaya çıkarılması ve adaletin sağlanması konusunda yaşanan sorunlara dikkat çekti.

Sosyal hizmet uzmanı Hilal Yılmaz ise kadınların ve çocukların karşı karşıya kaldığı olumsuz yaşam koşullarını somut örneklerle anlattı. Kadınların ve çocukların yaşadığı sorunların toplumsal boyutuna ve sosyal destek mekanizmalarının önemine değindi.

Panelde söz alan bir kadın arkadaşımız, Digel Tekstil ve Temel Conta işçilerinin direnişlerinden örnekler vererek işçi kadınların işyerlerinde yaşadıkları sorunlara dikkat çekti. Kadınların çalışma yaşamında karşılaştıkları eşitsizlikler, hak gaspları ve mücadele deneyimleri de panelin önemli başlıklarından biri oldu.

Panel, kadınların soruları, katkıları ve karşılıklı paylaşımlarıyla devam etti. Katılımcılar hem kendi deneyimlerini paylaşma hem de merak ettikleri konularda sorularını yöneltme fırsatı buldu.

Panelde şu ifadelere yer verildi:

“Aydın Ekmek ve Gül olarak bir kez daha vurguluyoruz: Kadınların yaşam hakkı, eşitlik ve özgürlük mücadelesi birbirinden ayrılamaz. Evde, sokakta ve işyerinde kadınların karşılaştığı şiddete, eşitsizliğe ve sömürüye karşı mücadelemizi büyütüyoruz. Mirabel Kardeşlerden bugüne uzanan mücadele tarihimizden aldığımız güçle kadın dayanışmasını büyütmeye devam edeceğiz. Yaşamak için ekmek, ruhumuz için gül istiyoruz!”

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Unknown
title: Graham Purchase - Kropotkin and the Rise of Revolutionary Anarchism
content:
Author

: Graham Purchase

Title

: Kropotkin and the Rise of Revolutionary Anarchism

Subtitle

: Review

Date

: 2001, April

Source

: Scanned from Anarcho-Syndicalist Review 31 (April 2001)


 a review of


 Kropotkin and the Rise of Revolutionary Anarchism 1872-1886, by Caroline Cahm, Cambridge University Press, 1989.


 This excellent work of modern scholarship focuses upon a specific period of Kropotkin's life, 1872-1886, during which he was intensely involved in the development and propagation of European anarchism, through his actions, speeches and articles. This period of intense activism lies between Kropotkin's earlier involvement with Russian populism and his long exile in England, where he wrote the many longer books for which he remains famous today.


 During these years he travelled widely throughout Western Europe, living for long periods in Switzerland (expelled 1881) and France, where he was imprisoned for three years (1883-6). Kropotkin's travels to countries with strong anarchist movements such as Belgium and Spain influenced his thinking. He also participated in anarchist conferences in Switzerland, Germany and London.


 His achievements during this period were many and varied. Shortly after arriving in Switzerland he enthusiastically took part in a demonstration involving illegally carrying the red flag in honor of the Paris Commune. The success of the Berne demonstration rejuvenated, for a short time, the Jura federation which had fallen into decline since the death of Bakunin and his own internment in a Russian prison. This point in time also saw the beginning of Kropotkin's journalistic career. He contributed quite a number of articles to the Bulletin of the Jura Federation of the IWA during 1876-7. These articles were never published in English, nor since republished in French.


 The value of Cahm's study is that it thoroughly examines important themes within this early journalism. Eminent scholars of Kropotkin, such as Martin Miller, regard Kropotkin's writings for the Bulletin and Rebel as some of his "best" and most "neglected." This neglect is a pity, for although about half of his contributions to the Bulletin were reports upon Russian affairs, primarily the trial of 1893, the other half include interesting and important contributions upon the ills of imperialism, parliamentary socialism and Marxism, a three-part analysis of the ills of British unionism, and articles upon U.S. labor issues.


 In 1879, following the collapse of the Bulletin and L'Avant Garde (to which he contributed one article on the Pittsburgh strikes), Kropotkin founded, edited and contributed to a new newspaper, Rebel (Le Revolte), published at Geneva until 1885. Although Kropotkin's first political book Words of a Rebel (Paris 1885, edited and compiled by Reclus), contains a very readable selection of the leading articles from the Rebel, there are a few, particularly concerning unionism which might also have been reasonably included. There are also other minor articles, such as those dealing with the value and desirability of direct-action strike tactics as a method of reversing reformist parliamentary unionism in Britain and France, which are also of interest in this respect. Again Cahm, in focusing attention upon his neglected works upon the subject of reformist and revolutionary unionism, provides a valuable resource upon which to better assess Kropotkin's thinking upon these issues. This scholarship is very valuable as his complex and interesting viewpoints concerning syndicalism, unionism and anarchism have been obscured by anarchist-communist scholars with anti-syndicalist prejudices.


 Towards the end of the period under review (1872-1886) Kropotkin took a central role in the defence at the Lyon Trial of 1883, which led to the imprisonment for several years of most of France's leading anarchists, including Kropotkin himself, in a farcical display of state-justice, which, for a short time at least, led to widespread public sympathy for the prisoners and what they stood for. The imprisonment of the most active anarchists and the subsequent intense state repression of the movement meant that little remained upon his release in 1886 when he began his long exile from continental Europe in England, where he could no longer take an active part in its affairs (though he helped found and finance two subsequent French-language newspapers to which he contributed scores of articles over the next 30 years).

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Anarchism, The Star of the Antipodes
content:
by Christian Ferrer


Revista Ají

, 24/05/2020


Nothing is more mysterious than the fate of anarchism, an ideal that might seem far-fetched were it not for the fact that it is extremely sensible. Although the passage of time has dimmed its lustre, and it was even declared extinct, the “libertarian cause” has continued to demonstrate its tenacity, as anarchists seem to possess the qualities of the phoenix – the ability to be reborn from their own ashes – like avatars that are reincarnated in various neighbouring spheres and offshoots. The anarchist ideal, while once politically and culturally prominent, remains incomprehensible in our times unless one first turns the world upside down. In truth, anarchy has always had a bad press—right from the start—: a “utopia”; a messianic call, then, something wild, at times otherworldly, always piercing.


Do as you please, live as you would like people to live in the future, do not join the military, do not eat animal carcasses, you are the king’s enemy, abhor prisons, glorify sex, stand your ground, do not obey or give orders, do not humiliate and do not let yourself be humiliated, do not leave a comrade in the lurch, better an outcast than a leader, you may take sides and be part of the action but do not form a party, borders are false and the law a fiction exploited by the powerful, love is free and long live loss. Such are the slogans, or counterbalances, the decalogue of antagonism and wonder. As for the anarchists, they were said to be scarecrows, and at times the label was deserved.


It is pointless to weigh up their actions, ups and downs, and achievements solely by the yardstick that measures success or failure, because the very fact that “the Idea” – as they called the sum of their principles – has appeared in the world remains a mystery of history. It does not seem a natural occurrence. Generally speaking, even if reluctantly, people come to terms with the world as it is, soothing their inevitable unease with benefits, subsidies and a few public holidays throughout the gruelling working year. Few are those who seek to turn it on its head in the blink of an eye. Pyramids, too, are built to be climbed, not to be torn down, stone by stone. Anarchism can be seen as an unusual, forceful and unyielding response to the existence of powers separate from the community, no less than to the obstacles and prohibitions placed in the way of the will to personal self-creation—in short, to everything that discourages or derails the mad desire to live, and that is precisely why the anarchist creed advocated a multifaceted revolution: cultural, psychological and political all at once. It was to ask a great deal; it was to be overly rational; it was to live without fear, with or without organisation; it was to enjoy the feast, in unity, at least while the affinity lasted. No more than that, no less than that.


From the very beginnings of anarchism, when Proudhon, Bakunin and Kropotkin laid the foundations, various branches and offshoots very quickly emerged, each emphasising, in its own way, different aspects: mutualism, collectivism, free love, concern for the fate of nature, vegetarianism, trade unionism, individualism, religiosity without established churches, spontaneism, women’s emancipation, morality without dogma, experimental communes and a number of other challenges that, in their day, seemed risky, if not “flowers of evil”: a scent at times sharp, at others sensual, always diverse and inventive. It is also worth highlighting anarchism’s ability to influence people, ideas and groups—and sometimes crowds—who did not necessarily identify as anarchists but who felt ‘”called” to sympathise with these principles or to reconsider their own convictions. In every case, hierarchical power was regarded as a human catastrophe, an enemy of lives that might otherwise have been less oppressed.


The opponents of anarchism are well known: the clergy, the powerful, the military, the employers, the “patriots”, those in power – not to mention the communists, their old enemies from before the now-forgotten Soviet Union even existed. These opponents knew that libertarian thought emphasised issues and problems that could not be resolved within the system of domination as it stood, including, amongst others, its very early critique of technology and industrialism, its warnings about ecological excesses, its exhortations to break away from failed emotional relationships, its advocacy of sexual …

author: Freedom Editor
title: Microscopic mutual aid
content:
From the deepest root to the highest leaf and every acorn, bacteria and fungi cooperate with each other and their host to survive

1.8 billion years ago the mitochondria, “the powerhouse of the cell,” moved within a host cell for protection. Neither side was exploited, and equilibrium was achieved. To this day, DNA is segregated between the mitochondria and the nucleus reminding us of cellular cooperation.

In her work, On the Origin of Mitosing Cells (1967), Lynn Margulis posited that structures such as the mitochondria originated from smaller specialised cells taking refuge within larger cells. 60 years after Kropotkin, Margulis’ Endosymbiotic Theory challenged the expectations of Darwinian evolution and was rejected by 15 journals. Endosymbiosis is now a respected cornerstone of evolutionary biology.

Our cells and ecosystems exemplify cooperation, not competition. Mutual aid is the biochemical basis of multicellular life meeting required energy demands; the mitochondria was a volunteer, but now it is part of the cooperative powerhouse of the cell(s).

I research microbiomes of terrestrial plants, using advanced molecular techniques to untangle form and function in microscopic communities.

Mutual aid has been the foundation of my research. From the deepest root to the highest leaf and every acorn, bacteria and fungi cooperate with each other and their host to survive, ward off disease, and improve overall wellbeing. If natural selection is the play, molecular mutual aid is the stage, the lights, the assistant, the director, and the crowd.

Microbiomes are complex systems that include beneficial, neutral or pathogenic individuals. As scientific knowledge expands, we are beginning to understand that the difference between a beneficial and detrimental microbe could be triggered by environmental stress. The shift is not governed by a central mechanism, but by a quorum of functionally cooperative bacteria following a unifying imperative: “common survival at all costs”.

Capitalism is fundamentally Darwinian: proliferate or perish, outcompete your rivals, grow exponentially. However, bacteria have shown us that natural selection is not exponential, and neither should be our methods of measuring economic progress.

The Escherichia coli (E. coli) Long-Term Evolution Experiment (LTEE) is the clearest demonstration of natural selection to date. Founded by Richard Lenski of Michigan State University in 1988, LTEE has observed the equivalent of more than 2,000,000 years of human evolution over 75,000 generations taking advantage of the rapid rate of replication in E. coli. Every day 1% fractions of the previous community are transferred into fresh medium; each day represents more than six generations.

Using molecular techniques, the group was able to track the rate of evolution within their E. coli lineages. They predicted that rate of evolution would be hyperbolic: a period of exponential development followed by a plateau, an upper ceiling. However, it was discovered that there is no upper ceiling. Exponential improvement in E. coli fitness is succeeded by incremental developments. Adaptations become exponentially rarer but never cease.

Put simply, evolutionary adaptations become less dramatic, the return on investment diminishes as the E. coli was already adapted to a cosy temperature of 37°C for the equivalent of 2,000,000 human years.

On our own, human scale, we have seen epochs of exponential growth, such as the industrial or agricultural revolutions, where outputs were tangible and material. Accelerationists wish you to believe that the incessant integration of the latest greatest technology – currently AI – will usher in a new revolution despite diminishing returns. But we are already at the point of diminishing returns. Why are data centres becoming larger instead of smaller and more efficient? Why is my chocolate bar shrinking? Culturally, how much did music change between 1960-90, compared to between 1990-2020?

I have seen in my own data that pathogenic fungi are often present and quantifiable up to 25% of community composition, but no signs of disease are present. Certainly, there are outright pathogens that cause disease. But if you placed them in a hermetically sealed box with their host, their long-term existence is not feasible. They infect, they multiply, the host dies, their population dies after consuming all the resources.

Exponential growth of a singular microbe is the hallmark of disease, and we …

title: Groupe de parole & d'organisation anarchiste contre l'inceste
content:
Groupe de parole & d'organisation anarchiste contre l'inceste


On vous invite chaleureusement à notre prochain groupe de parole et d'organisation anarchiste contre l'inceste, qui se tiendra le vendredi 27 novembre à partir de 18h30 au

CICP

, 21 rue Voltaire, 75011, Paris (salle verte, 1

er

 étage).


Puisque l'inceste nous concerne tous.tes, mais aussi parce que s'y reconnaître n'est pas toujours chose facile, l'espace est ouvert à tous.tes. On pourra se scinder en deux si besoin : un groupe de parole + un groupe d'organisation.


L'idée du groupe de parole


Elle part de nos besoins : celui de casser les silences qui nous détruisent, en parlant collectivement d'inceste. Mais aussi celui de se reconnaître pour s'entraider face à la famille, au trauma, aux institutions, face aussi à la vie qui ne nous épargne pas, voire face à nous-même et à la reproduction des violences que nous avons subies.


L'idée du groupe d'organisation


Elle part de notre envie de diffuser une culture de lutte contre l'inceste, d'organiser des événements publics, de faire de l'agitation autour du sujet, des tags, d'écrire ou de dessiner ensemble pour faire des tracts, des revues, des livres ou des podcasts, ou toute autre chose qui nous paraîtra nécessaire et nous fera envie

 

!


Pourquoi un groupe anarchiste contre l'inceste

 

?


Il existe de nombreux groupes de parole et d'organisation contre l'inceste qui basculent souvent dans le développement personnel ou dans l'organisation autour de leaders ou de figures individuelles (pour ne citer que ces deux exemples). On a envie de pouvoir attaquer la famille, l'État, la police et la justice et on a envie de faire les choses par nous-mêmes. Politiser l'inceste nous paraît être une donnée essentielle de notre démarche puisque le système-inceste se fonde sur l'autorité familiale, la domination adulte et/ou patriarcale. On avait envie de pouvoir tisser des discussions qui nous ressemblent et de développer ensemble une analyse politique à la fois pragmatique et radicale contre l'inceste.


Amène de la nourriture à partager si tu peux

 

!


Hâte de vous y voir

 

!


Des incesté.es révolté.es

content:
Πολυτεχνείο: Παρέμβαση αναρχικών στην κατάθεση στεφανιών και προσκλητήριο νεκρών αγωνιστ(ρι)ών μεταπολίτευσης (Βίντεο)


“Δεν υπάρχει μέρος που πεθαίνουν οι νεκροί, ζουν ανάμεσά μας”


Βίντεο

 και κέιμενο που λάβαμε και δημοσιεύουμε –


“Παρέμβαση ενάντια στην κατάθεση στεφανιού από το φασίστα Πρύτανη Χατζηγεωργίου, στην εκδήλωση μνήμης του ΣΦΕΑ, 17/11/2026.


Για πρώτη φορά, ακούγονται τα ονόματα των νεκρών αγωνιστ(ρι)ών της μεταπολίτευσης μαζί με αυτών της εξέγερσης του Πολυτεχνείου του ’73.


Ως Ανοιχτή Συνέλευση του κατειλλημένου Γκίνη “Μιχάλης Καλτεζάς” αποφασίσαμε συλλογικά να μην αφήσουμε τον φασίστα και βιαιολάτρη Πρύτανη Χατζηγεωργίου να καταθέσει στεφάνι την επέτειο της εξέγερσης του ’73.


Ενα σώμα περίπου 50 συντρόφων και συντροφισσών, αποτρέψαμε την εμφάνισή του, καθιστώντας σαφές πως είναι ανεπιθύμητος. Η παρέμβαση ήταν άκρως επιτυχημένη, καθώς το σώμα απαίτησε να ανοίξει η πύλη, ώστε ο κόσμος να μπει ξανά μέσα στο

Πολυτεχνείο

 και να τιμήσει τη μνήμη των νεκρών. Αφού εισήλθαμε ξανά στο συγκρότημα και εξασφαλίσαμε τη μη παρουσία του πρύτανη Χατζηγεωργίου, διεκδικήσαμε από το ΣΦΕΑ να διαβαστούν μετά τα ονόματα των νεκρών της εξέγερσης του Πολυτεχνείου, τα ονόματα των νεκρών αγωνιστ(ρι)ών της μεταπολίτευσης, τα οποία και διαβάζονται κατά το προσκλητήριο νεκρών στο σημείο της δολοφονίας του Μιχάλη Καλτεζά (Στουρνάρα και Μπουμπουλίνας).


Ήταν ένα ιστορικό τριήμερο για το αναρχικό/αντιεξουσιαστικό κίνημα και το κίνημα εν γένει, απόδειξη ότι η αυτοοργάνωση, η συντροφικότητα και η αλληλεγγύη θρέφουν το δέντρο της αντίστασης και της ατομικής και συλλογικής απελευθέρωσης. Πάντα στον δρόμο του αντικρατικού αγώνα χωρίς κηδεμόνες και αφεντικά, χωρίς περιορισμούς και κανόνες, προς την κοινωνική απελευθέρωση και την πλήρη ελευθερία. Ιδανικά που παίρνουν μεγαλύτερη αξία όταν βρίσκουν ανθρώπους που έχουν τη χαρά και την οργή αλλά και τη συνείδηση για έναν νέο κόσμο ισότητας και αδελφοσύνης.

Эти учебные вопросы разработаны Geelong Anarchist-communists (GAC) и могут использоваться на учебных кружках по этой брошюре. GAC решили задавать вопросы только по существенному содержанию брошюры и не углубляться далее в исторические аспекты первой и третьей глав. Поэтому вопросов по этим главам нет.

II. Социальный анархизм, классовая борьба и Центро-Периферические отношения

1. Что такое идеология согласно ФАРЖ? Согласны ли вы с такой трактовкой? Почему?

2. Что такое политическая практика согласно ФАРЖ? Согласны ли вы с его определением? Почему?

3. Какую критику анархизм получил, в частности, от Малатесты и Фаббри? Согласны ли вы с этой критикой? Почему?

4. Что такое социальный анархизм согласно ФАРЖ?

5. Что такое «центр-периферия» и чему она служит? Согласны ли вы с ней? Почему?

IV. Общество господства и эксплуатации: Капитализм и государство

1. Согласны ли вы с определением господства и эксплуатации у ФАРЖ? Почему?

2. Как ФАРЖ определяет различные виды труда – интеллектуальный и ручной? Согласны ли вы с такими определениями?

3. Почему ФАРЖ дистанцируется от использования государства как средства социальной и экономической революции? Как они определяют понятие государства?

V. Конечные цели: Социальная Революция и Либертарный социализм

1. Что ФАРЖ понимают под социальной революцией? Почему это важно?

2. Каковы задачи социальной революции согласно ФАРЖ?

3. Какие социальные/экономические изменения ФАРЖ считают приоритетными?

4. Как должны приниматься коллективные решения в либертарно-социалистическом обществе согласно ФАРЖ?

VI. Организация и социальная сила

author: Radikal Perspektif
title: William Godwin’in Eğitim Üzerine Düşünceleri
content:
Yazan: Mark K. Smith


Çeviren: Gorthim


Çevirilen Asıl Metin


PDF Linki


William Godwin

 (1756 – 1836), “anarşist ilkeleri net bir şekilde ortaya koyan” ilk yazardı (Marshall 1993: 191). Devlet kontrolündeki eğitimin tehdidini fark eden ve alternatif, özgür bir eğitimin özelliklerini ortaya koyan ilk İngilizce yazarlardan biriydi. Günümüzde o, belki de en çok Mary Wollstonecraft’ın (feminist bir klasik olan Kadın Haklarının Savunması -1792 kitabının yazarı) eşi, Mary Shelley’nin (Frankenstein – 1818 kitabının yazarı) babası ve şair Percy Bysshe Shelley’nin (radikal liberterliğinden etkilenen) kayınpederi olarak hatırlanmaktadır.


Hayatı


William Godwin’in hayatı şüphesiz inişler ve çıkışlarla doluydu. Bir

Dissenter

1

 ailesinde dünyaya gelen Godwin, aşırı bir Kalvinist olan Samuel Newton tarafından bireysel olarak (ve bazen acımasızca) eğitildi. Daha sonra (17 yaşındayken) Hoxton’daki Dissenting Academy’ye katıldı. Başlangıçta rahiplik mesleğine girmek isteyen Godwin, zamanla kendini “tamamen inançsız” olarak tanımlamaya başladı. Muhafazakârlığı, cumhuriyetçiliğe dönüştü. Bu sonuçlara mantık yoluyla ulaştığı anlaşılıyor. Radikal görüşleri, Rousseau gibi yazarlarla tanışması ve Amerikan Bağımsızlık Savaşı gibi siyasi olaylardan kaynaklanıyordu.


Ruhbanlıktan uzaklaşan William Godwin, yazarlık ve öğretmenlikle geçimini sağladı. Yazıları arasında kısa romanlar, biyografiler ve gazete makaleleri yer alıyordu. Fransız Devrimi’ni (1789’dan itibaren) çevreleyen şiddetli tartışma ve çekişmelere yanıt olarak Godwin, siyasi teoriye dair tam anlamıyla felsefi ve ilkeli bir açıklama ortaya koymak istedi. Bunun sonucu, 1793’te yayımlanan

Siyasi Adalet Üzerine Bir İnceleme

 adlı eserdi. Bu eser ona geçici bir şöhret ve bir miktar servet (bin gine) kazandırdı. Godwin, 1794’te bunu

The Adventures of Caleb Williams

 adlı bir romanla takip etti. Peter Marshall, bu romanı “hükümetin ruhu ve karakterinin toplumun her kesimine nasıl müdahale ettiğini” göstermek üzere tasarlanmış “kaçış ve kovalamacadan oluşan sürükleyici bir hikâye” olarak tanımlamaktadır. Kitap bir başyapıt olarak alkışlandı. “Bu eser sadece parlak bir toplumsal gözlem eseri olmakla kalmaz, aynı zamanda modern varoluşçuluğun kaygılarını öngören ilk gerilim romanı ve ilk psikolojik roman olarak da değerlendirilebilir” (1993: 196).


Bu sıralarda William Godwin, Mary Wollstonecraft ile tanıştı ve ikisi sevgili oldular. Hamile kaldığında Wollstonecraft, Godwin’den kendisiyle evlenmesini istedi (Godwin, evlilik kurumuna derin bir eleştiri getirse de 1797’de bu isteği kabul etti – bu özel durumda “faydaların” “zararlarından” daha ağır bastığına inanıyordu). Bu dönemde (Somerstown’daki 27 The Polygon adresinde yaşarken) oldukça mutlu görünüyordu – ancak bu mutluluk kısa sürdü. Wollstonecraft, kızı Mary’yi doğururken hayatını kaybetti.


William Godwin yazmaya devam etti; ancak entelektüel ve siyasi akımlar aleyhine işliyordu. 1801’de komşusu Mary Jane Clairmont ile yeniden evlendi. Birlikte Hanway Caddesi’nde (1805’te) bir Çocuk Kütüphanesi kurdular. Bir dizi öncü çocuk kitabı ürettiler; bunların bazıları Godwin tarafından, çoğu ise başka yazarlar tarafından yazılmıştı ve Hanway Caddesi’ndeki dükkandan yayınlandı. Daha sonra işlerini Holborn’a taşıyacaklardı; ancak sürekli mali sorunlarla boğuşuyorlardı ve borçları artıyordu. Yazı işlerinden elde ettikleri gelir giderek azalıyordu. Sonunda bir emekli maaşı kabul etmek zorunda kaldı. 77 yaşında Ofis Sorumlusu ve Yeoman Usher oldu ve New Palace Yard’da (Parlamento Binaları’nın yanında) bir konaklama yeri tahsis edildi. Marshall’ın da belirttiği gibi: “Godwin’in karmaşık hayatının en büyük ironisi, ortadan kaldırılmasını istediği, artık işlevini yitirmiş bir kurumun bakımını üstlenerek günlerini sonlandırmasıydı” (1993: 200). 1836’da vefat etti ve kendi isteği üzerine Mary Wollstonecraft’ın yanına gömüldü.


Anarşizm


Woodcock’a (1963: 57) göre, William Godwin’in felsefesi bir anarşist doktrinin tüm temel özelliklerini barındırıyordu. O:


Hükümete dayalı her türlü toplumsal sistemi reddetti.


Maddi malların gönüllü paylaşımına dayanan, otoritenin giderek azaldığı, basitleştirilmiş ve ademi merkeziyetçi bir toplumla ilgili kendi kavrayışını ortaya koydu.


Her türlü siyasi parti veya siyasi amaçtan bağımsız bir propaganda yoluyla bu hedefe ulaşmak için kendi yöntemini önerdi. (Woodcock 1963: 57)


Siyasi Adalet

, etik önkabullerden siyasi sonuçlar çıkaran, özenle gerekçelendirilmiş bir argümandır. Yazar …

title: Intensify, Disrupt, Sabotage, De-bank, Abolish & Liberate* – Solidarität mit Daniel V. [de+eng]
content:
* “Disrupt, Identify, Defund, Debank, Arrest & Prosecute”: Trump-Regierung droht linken Gruppen in einem Interview des US-Außenministeriums.


Disclaimer: Leider können viele Informationen über Daniel V. und die von ihm übernommenen Verantwortungen nicht bestätigt werde, da die meisten der „zugänglichen“ Quellen in den Händen der deutschen Medien liegen. Da sein Brief nie vollständig veröffentlicht wurde, können wir keine akkuraten Informationen wiedergeben und wir haben entschieden, nicht für ihn zu sprechen. Obwohl wir versucht haben, so viele Informationen aus online Quellen wie möglich zusammen zu sammeln, können wir deren Richtigkeit nicht garantieren und bitten die Lesenden nichts als definitiv hinzunehmen.


In verschiedenen Kämpfen intensiviert sich die Repression gegen jene, die Widerstand leisten. Von der Solidarität mit Palästina und Widerstand gegen die Militarisierung, zu militantem Antifaschismus und direkter Aktion – der Staat breitet seine Werzeuge aus, um diejenigen zu verfolgen, einzuschüchtern und zu isolieren, welche seine Autorität in Frage stellen. Unter dem öffentlich ausgerufenen Krieg gegen „Linksextremismus“ [1] wird Widerstand zunehmend als so schnell wie möglich zu eliminierende Bedrohung behandelt. Diese Entwicklung ist Teil einer breiteren autoritären und faschistischen Verschiebung, in welcher die Sprache und die Praxis der extremen Rechten die politische Agenda über verschiedene Grenzen hinweg prägt. Repression richtet sich gegen Demonstrationen, Selbstorganisation, Solidarität, Sabotage und jeden Versuch, die Legitimität der Machttragenden zu hinterfragen. Die reformistischen Grenzen dessen, was als „akzeptable Opposition“ erachtet wird werden ständig neu gezogen und die Widerständigen werden fortgehend als Kriminelle, Extremisten, Terroristen oder Mitglieder sogenannter krimineller Organisationen bezeichnet. Dies passiert oft bereits schon bevor die Öffentlichkeit erfährt was passiert ist, indem die politischen Motivationen, die hinter deren Aktionen stecken zensiert und unsichtbar gemacht werden.


Am 8. September 2026 wurde Daniel V. aufgrund mehrerer Sabotageakte in der Nähe eines Kohlekraftwerks bei Aachen verhaftet. Kurze Zeit nachdem seine Mutter in ihrem Zuhause von Journalisten interviewt wurde, wurde das Haus in dem sie mit Daniel lebt durchsucht. Außerdem gab es eine Razzia im Hambacher Forst und die dort lebenden Besetzer*innen wurden von der Bullenpräsenz und ihren Drohnen belästigt. Ein paar Tage zuvor hatte Daniel V. einen Brief an eine Zeitung gesendet, in welchem er die Verantwortung für mehrere Aktionen in unterschiedlichen Bundesländern übernommen hat, darunter Nordrhein-Westfalen und Brandenburg. Die Aktionen zu denen sich Daniel bekannte sorgten für Kurzschlüsse und vorübergehende Stromausfälle. Dafür feuerte er selbsterfundene und -gebaute Raketen in Hochspannungsleitungen. In diesem Text streben wir nicht an, die von Daniel verwendeten Taktiken zu analysieren, sondern stattdessen den Fokus auf die Art der darauf folgenden Repressionen zu legen und sie in den breiteren Kontext des Terrors zu stellen, der vom rechten Regime ausgeht.


Kurz nach dem 1. September wurde eine großangelegte Fahndung losgetreten – wieder einmal begleitet von den Taktiken des sozialen Kannibalismus, welcher die Menschen dazu anregen soll sich gegenseitig ans Messer zu liefern, um eine Belohnung zu erhalten, während die Medien mit ihrer Performance weiter machten. Daniel hat sich dazu entschlossen, sein Statement (hier die erste Seite seines Briefs: https://kontrapolis.info/18718/) an die Zeitung TAZ [2] zu senden. Anstatt Daniels eigene Worte zu veröffentlichen, entschied sich die TAZ einen eigenen Artikel über ihn zu schreiben und somit zu dem breiteren journalistischen Narrativ beizutragen, welches ihn als Psycho oder Terroristen porträtiert. Eine Zeitung, die Stolz darauf war den Tisch [3] der Kommune 1 [4] im Hinterhof zu haben und zu behaupten Teil einer linken Bewegung zu sein.


Dieses Narrativ ist Teil einer generelleren Tendenz der Medien, Menschen als psychologisch instabil, irrational oder gefährlich darzustellen, anstatt die wahren Gesichter des Widerstands und die Niederlagen des Staates und die Unfähigkeit sich selbst zu verteidigen anzuerkennen. Durch den Entschluss der Nicht-Veröffentlichung von Daniels Statement, hat die TAZ mal wieder gezeigt, dass die etablierten und kommerziellen Medien nicht als Teil irgendeiner Bewegung von unten angesehen werden können und dies …

author: Novara Media
title: The Truth About Xinjiang
content:
Xinjiang is one of the most fought-over stories in the world. Beijing says the place’s transformation is a story of modernisation and counter-terrorism. Human Rights Watch, Amnesty and the UN’s human rights office have all describes mass internment and possible crimes against humanity.


So what is actually happening there and who can you trust?


Darren Byler is a socialist anthropologist who did his fieldwork in Ürümqi, the region’s capital.


He talks to Richard Hames about Uyghur life before the crackdown, the surveillance system that spans from tracking software on phones to continuous checkpoints to security service agents living in Uyghurs’ houses. He describes the camps and system of forced labour, and why he calls the whole system “terror capitalism”, a frontier where settler colonialism merges with the tech industry.

title: Reuben Rose-Redwood, Wil Sahar Patrick - Why activists are vandalizing statues to colonialism
content:
Author

: Reuben Rose-Redwood, Wil Sahar Patrick

Title

: Why activists are vandalizing statues to colonialism

Date

: March 17 2020

Source

: Retrieved on November 14 2026 from https://theconversation.com/why-activists-are-vandalizing-statues-to-colonialism-129750


 In 2018, statues of

Edward Cornwallis

 and

John A. Macdonald

 were removed from their respective pedestals in Halifax and Victoria. Across Canada, colonial statues

have also been vandalized

 as an act of protest.


 Statues and monuments have become major

flashpoints

 of political conflict over the past decade.


 After the 2015

Charleston Massacre

, in which a neo-Confederate white supremacist murdered nine African Americans at the Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Charleston, South Carolina, a movement to remove

Confederate monuments and place names

 swept across the United States.


 Another wave of Confederate statue removals and place renamings occurred in the

aftermath

 of the Unite the Right rally in Charlottesville, Virginia in 2017.


 In South Africa, the

#RhodesMustFall movement

 led to the removal of a statue honoring the British imperialist Cecil Rhodes at the University of Cape Town in 2015. This inspired efforts to challenge Rhodes’s legacy

elsewhere

 as well.


A crowd looks on as the statue of imperialist Cecil Rhodes is removed from its perch at the University of Cape Town in 2015. Schalk van Zuydam


 Monument controversies are not unique to the 21st century.

Commemorative landscapes

 have been radically transformed during political regime changes throughout history. Following the Second World War, monuments to the Nazi regime

were toppled

. Similarly, the

fall of the Soviet Union

 and the

end of apartheid in South Africa

 led to significant changes to the memorial landscape.


The Legacies of Settler Colonialism


Settler colonialism

 is a process of colonization based upon the replacement of Indigenous or colonized peoples with a settler society. This involves both the disposession of Indigenous land and the erasure, either through assimilation or elimination, of Indigenous peoples.


 Colonial statues and place names are part of the political infrastructure of settler place-making in Canada. As a result, they have become focal points for challenging settler-colonial power and testing the limits of reconciliation.


 On Jan. 31, 2018, the Cornwallis statue was taken down from its pedestal in Halifax. As an honorific commemoration for the “founder” of Halifax, Mi'kmaw elders

have long viewed

 the statue as a sign of the ongoing dispossession of Indigenous peoples and called for its removal.


 As if answering the East Coast, the John A. Macdonald statue was removed from the entrance to City Hall in Victoria on Aug. 11, 2018. The decision to remove the Macdonald statue was made as part of the city’s

formal reconciliation process

 with the Songhees and Esquimalt First Nations.


 As Canada’s first prime minister, Macdonald was chief architect of its residential school system and promoted genocidal policies against Indigenous peoples. His monumental presence at the entrance to City Hall was a major barrier to reconciliation efforts.


 In August 2018, a second plaque was installed to replace a bronze statue of Canada’s first Prime Minister John A. Macdonald after the first was vandalized shortly after the removal of the statue from the front of City Hall in Victoria, BC. Chad Hipolito/THE CANADIAN PRESS


 A year later, the city of New Westminster followed suit, removing a statue of the

“Hanging Judge” Matthew Begbie

 from the grounds of the provincial courthouse.


 Those opposed to the removal of statues often propose adding historic plaques as a way to recontextualize statues while leaving them in public spaces. Some activists, however, have chosen a different option: vandalism.


Vandalizing Colonial Statues and Monuments


 Across Canada, contentious statues and monuments linked to settler colonialism have been targeted with vandalism. In Montréal, the

John A. Macdonald and Queen Victoria monuments

 have been regularly spray-painted. Macdonald statues have been vandalized in

Kingston

 and

Regina

 as far back

as 2012

.


 Accompanying the campaign to remove the Cornwallis statue in Halifax were several

incidents

 of

vandalism

 as well.


 These are not random acts of hooliganism. The vandalism of colonial statues is an expression of political protest against the …

author: The Elephant
title: Alternative Leadership As A Decolonial Paradigm
content:
Sarova Stanley, Nairobi | 11 November 2026


Theme: Reimagining Leadership, Reclaiming Citizen Agency


Dr. Kawive Wambua;


The leadership and team of Inuka Kenya Ni Sisi!;

Representatives of civil society;

Distinguished guests;

Fellow Kenyans:


Good morning.


Thank you for inviting me to join you at the launch of the Inuka! Angaza Kura Campaign.


Your theme, “Reimagining Leadership, Reclaiming Citizen Agency,” brings us to the central question of our democracy: The Constitution proclaims Sovereignty of the people, but who truly exercises power in Kenya?


Is it the citizen whose taxes sustain the state, whose labour builds the economy, and whose vote confers authority? Or is it the officeholder who, once elected, hijacks power and behaves like the master, relegating citizens to subjects?


What must the citizens do to reclaim their agency, their power? 


You have asked me to reflect on “Alternative Leadership as a Decolonial Paradigm.”


The language may sound academic, but the issue is profoundly practical.


It concerns the relationship between a Kenyan citizen and the person entrusted to serve them. It concerns whether a police officer offers protection or inspires fear; whether a public office provides a service or demands a favour; whether public money builds opportunity or finances private privilege.


Above all, it concerns whether independence has become an everyday experience of dignity and quality services for us. 


From subjects to citizens


The colonial state was organised to control people and extract resources. Its authority flowed downwards. The population was expected to comply, while those who governed were insulated from meaningful accountability to the governed.


Independence was supposed to transform that relationship.


Yet changing the nationality of those occupying public office could not, by itself, dismantle the habits, incentives and institutions of domination, without changing the mindset of the office holders. Understanding leadership to be service and sacrifice, rather than entitlement and a life of privilege at the expense of basic needs for the people. Imagining leadership as an opportunity to ensure protection of the rights of the people and to uphold and affirm the dignity of the people you serve. Ensuring that, as a leader, you remain loyal to the purpose- service with openness and accountability. These are the minimum standards demanded by the constitution we gifted ourselves. 


Whenever leadership demands obedience without accountability, the colonial model or inheritance survives. Whenever citizens must seek political patronage to obtain public services, it survives. Whenever criticism is treated as disloyalty, it survives.


Decolonising leadership therefore requires us to confront the exercise of power in our own time.


We must ask whether the state serves citizens as people with rights, or manages them as subjects who should remain grateful for favours.


A hospital is a public responsibility. A road is a public investment. Education is an investment in the nation’s future. Every service by leaders is part of their duty to us, funded by our taxes, not a favour. 


None of these should become a personal gift for which citizens owe a politician their silence. Service should not be in exchange for citizens losing their freedom to exercise their right to demand accountability. Service must never be at the cost of citizens losing their agency, their power to oversee leaders, the government. 


An alternative must be radically different in word and deed. 


Comrades,


The word “alternative” carries an obligation.


Those of us who seek to offer alternative leadership must demonstrate how we would govern differently. We must affirm our allegiance to the Constitution, whose main objective is to restrain, or in other words, limit the exercise of power.  Alternative leadership must affirm citizens’ right to seek accountability and readiness to vacate office should citizens unequivocally so demand. The Alternative leadership must pledge allegiance to the Constitution and the people of Kenya, and affirm the sovereignty of the people. Demonstrate an understanding that leadership is a privilege to serve, not a title deed to rule over the people. Our utterances and actions as alternative leadership must so demonstrate. 


It is insufficient to condemn arrogance in government while practising it within our political parties. We cannot promise inclusion while silencing young …

author: Publicación Abierta
title: La derrota del trumpismo: ¿un canto de cisne o un cisne negro?
content:
LA DERROTA DEL TRUMPISMO: ¿UN

CANTO DE CISNE

 O UN

CISNE NEGRO

?


Por Rafael Bautista S.


Mientras el futuro más temible llegue,


lo único que nos devuelva la luz será


esta velita prendida que supimos


cuidar en plena oscuridad.


Ya con la cabeza fría, conviene profundizar analítica y prospectivamente lo que se ha de jugar en estos casi dos meses de transición hacia las más temibles opciones que se pondrán en movimiento, una vez que el Estado profundo ha decidido prescindir del episodio Trump. Por cuestiones de sobrevivencia discordante –como ya señalamos– entre dos opciones supremacistas de restauración del liderazgo imperial

[1]

, la derrota de Trump no limpia el panorama sino lo enrarece aún más.


Todos saben que los demócratas son rusóbos, para empezar, y eso no augura un cese de la amenaza nuclear sino la radicaliza, como ya se está observando en los últimos movimientos beligerantes de la OTAN, Inglaterra y Alemania

[2]

 contra Rusia. El AIPAC, por cuestiones ya de sobrevivencia del Estado sionista, más aún cuando perdió Netanyahu, hará uso de su fuerte influencia entre los demócratas

[3]

 para continuar la política nuclear contra Irán y el exterminio de los gazatíes y los palestinos en general (Líbano, Siria y Cisjordania). Lo cual, además de la prolongación del genocidio palestino, no hace sino continuar, por otros medios, la política expansiva (aunque cada vez menos posible, como la inutilidad de los bombardeos recientes de parte de USA e Israel a Irán) del Estado sionista.


Tampoco los inmigrantes verán otro panorama más alentador con los demócratas, cuando fue la administración “demócrata” de Obama, por ejemplo, la que más cantidad de deportados produjo. De boca para afuera, los demócratas harán de Trump el chivo expiatorio que necesita la restauración imperial para justificar su continuidad. Creyendo que la limpieza de la imagen imperial podrá ofrecerle demagógicamente al mundo, otra cosa que no sea una nueva versión de la continuidad de “un mundo basado en reglas” para los demás y excepciones para el Imperio.


En ese contexto, pondremos a consideración el panorama que sugiere Alexander Dugin y nuestro comentario a lo que creemos, una de las descripciones más cercanas a lo que se viene. En sus propias palabras

[4]

, si Trump pierde irremediablemente el control del Congreso: “la venganza de los demócratas contra Trump y sus seguidores

no se parecerá a nada de lo que hemos visto antes

”. Los demócratas no pasarán por alto, lo que significó el desmantelamiento de los brazos administrativos y operativos de su poder de influencia nacional y global, cuando se creó la Oficina de Eficiencia Gubernamental, el DOGE, y se inició la desarticulación de la Agencia de los Estados Unidos para el Desarrollo Internacional, la USAID (desde donde se operó la restauración derechista –una vez desarticulada por la “primavera democrática”– en Latinoamérica, en favor de la tutela demócrata gringa). Esa era una de las vías que permitió la injerencia de los intereses que representa, por ejemplo, George Soros. Por eso, no es casual la sincronía de la ola de protestas en Europa

[5]

 y el triunfo demócrata en USA. Hasta el triunfo de Lula se explicaría, en parte, por esa caída de las piezas de dominó que sostenía al trumpismo, a nivel global (rival en la jefatura de un nuevo orden mundial que destaca otro tipo de intereses, sobre todo financieros, que tienen en Soros un actor reconocible).


Dugin, en tono de socarrón señala: “realmente creyeron que Trump cumpliría sus promesas y que el Estado profundo estaba a punto de ser erradicado de raíz”. Pero Trump, que nunca generó el contexto para la realización del golpe definitivo, ahora tiene, en el Congreso (tanto en diputados como en senadores, además de gobernadores), la mayoría necesaria para que el globalismo, que intentó atacar, reorganice filas con sus portavoces y comiencen el contraataque.


Ya algunos analistas en geopolítica preguntan si quien ganó en las “midterm” fue, en realidad, Soros. Pero éste es sólo el actor expuesto y si algo manifiesta el

poder duro

poder duro

author: Rose Nneoma Abba
title: Labors of liberation
content:
Ricci Shryock’s

The Moon Will Not Burn Us

 is marketed as an account of the women who helped win the 11-year guerrilla war for independence from Portuguese colonial rule in Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde. Shryock’s book delivers on that promise with hyperrealistic scenes that drop you into mangrove forests where female teenagers and young adults shoot and dodge bullets, manage makeshift clinics, become mothers, devise new cooking technology, teach, gossip, and boil water for breakfast. 

It also exposes prejudice that women in the struggle faced at the hands of their fellow African men. A funny scene in the book exemplifies both the prejudice and the women’s handling of it. Shortly after Joana Gomes, a nurse and the book’s protagonist, joins a new base, the commander, who is also her distant cousin, threatens her that if she gets hurt, he will have to kill her. She replies that “as a nurse. . . .  even you, if you are injured and no-one can carry you I can give this medicine to you [to kill you].” As Carmen Pereira, a prominent guerrilla fighter with the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), nurse, and later acting head of state, famously observed: “In Guinea-Bissau, we say that women must fight against two colonialisms. One against the Portuguese, the other against men.”

But beyond illustrating women’s agency in the struggle, the book also offers timely provocations on our relationship with nature, the labor that sustains revolutions, elite-led movements, and the individual costs of collective struggle.

One of the book’s greatest strengths is its exploration of how the PAIGC’s vision of a future state manifested in practice long before victory was formally declared. The PAIGC was founded in 1956 to achieve independence for Guinea and Cape Verde from Portuguese colonial rule. For the party, building for the future state was just as vital as tearing down Portuguese colonial rule. 

This state-building effort is most visible in the book’s heartwarming scenes of education. We witness it when Joana’s father goes out of his way to secure teachers for his daughters. And again when 11-year-old Joana and her friends are instructed by Amílcar Cabral to teach the other teenagers on a boat trip from Guinea-Bissau to Guinea-Conakry. We learn that the PAIGC built 156 primary schools during the war across liberated territories compared to 11 created under Portuguese neglect. We also see the PAIGC send young Guineans to the Soviet Union and Cuba to master guerrilla combat tactics as well as medicine, engineering, agronomy, and teaching for the nation they were bringing into existence.

The book takes a firm stand: The success of a liberation struggle depends on the viable, egalitarian alternative structure you build to ground your sovereignty while you fight the oppressive power. As Shryock writes in the introduction, it is “a story worth knowing as a universal lesson in the undeniable courage it takes to imagine a new world, the way creation rather than destruction is integral to that new world.” Through Joana’s story, Shryock holds a steady lens on women’s central role in designing and executing that vital labor of building Guinean sovereignty from the ground up.

Shryock opens the book with a scene that haunts the entire reading experience: 22-year-old Joana inside a dry-season mangrove forest, where she had gone to retrieve a commander who was recovering from a lung infection. “Gnarly, bare mangrove branches protruding from the muddy riverbed stare back at [Joana],” setting the tone for the book from the very first page. 

The land, its trees, and its waters are alive. At times angry, at times hungry, mostly gracious, and systematically exploited by the Portuguese regime. And it was precisely this ecological exploitation that precipitated the revolution. Cabral, the founder of the PAIGC, was an agronomist by training, and his radicalization took root while he was conducting an agricultural census commissioned by the United Nations and the colonial Portuguese government. There, he saw firsthand how Portuguese land policies and price controls were squeezing the life out of both the land and the people tilling it.

As the Guineans fought for the land, the land protected them. Whether it is Joana tripping over an exposed root and narrowly dodging a bullet or people abandoning their towns to seek shelter in the forest, “besides the Soviets and the Cubans, the land [proved] to be the liberation …

Given that we live in a society that promotes ignorance and superficiality, perhaps it shouldn’t be all that surprising that current day anarchist discussions of historic inter-anarchist debates usually miss the point when it comes to colonialism (and imperialism more generally.)

Anarchists do not somehow become immune to colonial society’s influence simply by making abstract and hollow declarations of opinion. Knowledge and comprehension require actual commitment and curiosity, and these are sadly rare qualities among the European, Euro-American and Euro-Canadian anarchists of today.

This article is an attempt at a brief analysis of what’s been missing in recent anarchist discussions of three historic inter-anarchist debates. The term “debates” is used here in the widest sense of a general disagreement rather than some formally-held event or correspondence. Specifically, I refer to the debates between Luigi Galleani and Ricardo Flores Magón over the Mexican Revolution, between Peter Kropotkin and Errico Malatesta on the First World War, and between Emma Goldman and Reginald Reynolds on Palestine.

In the case of Reynolds, we should note that he considered himself a fellow traveler and sympathizer of anarchism, wrote regularly for the anarchist periodicals edited by Vernon Richards, and married the socialist-turned-anarchist Ethel Mannin, but did not self-identify as an anarchist, so my phrase “inter-anarchist debate” must also be understood in the broadest sense.

The anarchist periodical Tinderbox and the anarchist website The Transmetropolitan Review (TTR) have recently invoked the Galleani-Magón debate, though without even being aware of it in the former case.

The individual who writes articles at the TTR website claimed in May of this year that the historic anarchist Partido Liberal Mexicano (PLM) made a “fateful alliance with Pascual Orozco,” the latter being a bourgeois revolutionary who, with the help of Pancho Villa, took control of Ciudad Juárez in 1911. The author makes no distinction between the on-the-ground forces of the PLM and the Junta (leadership board) of that organization, which, from Los Angeles obviously could not directly control the actions of every individual on the frontlines in Mexico, even if they had wanted to.

TTR goes on to sell the lie that at the time, “the PLM was willing to work with anyone against Madero, and they took positions in Orozco’s rebel government alongside oligarchs and hacienda owners, something which further isolated the PLM from anarchists.”

In reality, Magón and the rest of the Junta, in their periodical, Regeneración, called for violent resistance to Orozco once he took control of Juárez, denouncing him as bourgeois and openly accusing him of being on the wrong side of the revolution, specifically because he was trying to disarm other revolutionaries and was friendly with the rich.

To be clear where TTR wasn’t, the anarchists they claim the PLM isolated …

author: Keston K. Perry
title: The imperialism of progressive economics
content:
Progressive economics has an imperial problem. It is possible to denounce inequality, defend redistribution, and criticize neoliberalism while preserving a deeper hierarchy: the presumption that experts, often based in powerful institutions in the Global North, can determine what justice should mean for societies shaped by slavery, colonial extraction, and imperial rule. The issue is not simply whether their intentions are good or their proposals sufficiently radical. It is who has the power to define the problem, decide which histories count and prescribe solutions after short field visits or, worse, on conference calls, before those most affected have determined the terms of repair.

This contradiction is particularly visible in debates about reparations and climate finance. Universal basic income, public ownership, cheaper credit, and expanded development finance can all be useful demands. None, however, returns stolen land, reverses accumulated colonial wealth, repairs ecological destruction, or restores collective authority over political and economic life. Redistribution and reparations can reinforce one another; they are not interchangeable. When the former is offered as a substitute for the latter, progressive universalism becomes a way of setting aside historically specific claims.

I encountered this argument during a debate about reparations in 2020. A senior economist asked where reparative claims should begin and end, questioned the feasibility of identifying descendants of enslaved people, and suggested universal income or shared dividends funded by wealth taxes as more practicable responses. The framing exposes an asymmetry: Why must restitution meet an exceptional test of feasibility while universal redistribution is treated as a reasonable starting point? Who decides which demands are too complicated to count as politics?

The point is not to dismiss universal social provision. It is to insist that the injuries of empire cannot be reduced to unequal household incomes. Colonialism reorganized property, labor, public finance, land tenure, and the authority to govern. Repair must be capable of transforming those relationships, not merely compensating people for living within them.

At a conference on African economic sovereignty in Dakar in 2022, I heard related arguments from progressive economists who treated nationalization or the green developmental state as ready-made alternatives to reparations. State ownership and planning can be indispensable instruments of transformation. Yet our meeting in the Museum of Black Civilizations was a striking setting in which to overlook the intellectual traditions and struggles through which African peoples have articulated their own visions of sovereignty. A model developed in one context does not become universal because its advocates consider themselves anti-neoliberal. The question is who defines the political horizon, and whose knowledge is allowed to unsettle it.

A similar dilemma runs through the international sustainability industry. Island and African societies confronting climate disasters are surrounded by consultants, conveners, investment platforms, and intermediaries promising innovation. International collaboration is not inherently objectionable. What matters is who controls the agenda, data, networks, and resulting resources. When communities supply experiences while outsiders translate them into fundable or bankable projects, an old division of labor survives under the language of partnership.

The Bridgetown Initiative brings these contradictions into focus. Barbados Prime Minister Mia Mottley has rightly drawn attention to the global financial system’s unequal treatment of climate-vulnerable countries. The initiative has pushed sovereign debt, liquidity, Special Drawing Rights, and multilateral development bank reform onto an international agenda that too often marginalizes small states. Yet recognition of an unjust financial architecture is not the same as transforming the relations of ownership and creditor power that sustain it. Expanded access to finance can leave the underlying distribution of wealth, risk, and power largely intact.

Consider what financial innovation means when disaster strikes. After Hurricane Beryl in 2024, Grenada activated a disaster clause that deferred debt-service payments. This created fiscal breathing room, but deferred payments were added to principal: relief in the timing of repayment, not cancellation of the …

author: Unknown
title: Mangelhafte Recherche als Kritik verpackt
content:
Nach der Demo gegen Imperialismus vom 11. Oktober 2026 schrieb Noctua Rosa Moser einen Meinungsartikel bei "Dilemma" (ehemalig "Das Lamm). Statt einer differenzierten Perspektive oder einer solidarischen Kritik, setzte die Redakteur*in auf einen Kahlschlag gegen die Demo und die dahinterstehende Bewegung: Eine Gegenkritik.


Wir sind zwei der Bewegung vom 11. Oktober gegenüber solidarisch eingestellten Genoss*innen. In dieser Replik werden Inhalte des Textes von Noctua auf den Prüfstand gestellt. Ursprünglich war geplant, die Gegenkritik bei "Dilemma" selbst zu publizieren: das hat jedoch nicht geklappt, jedenfalls nicht so, dass die Bedürfnisse beider Seiten befriedigt gewesen wären. Das ist mitunter ein Grund, warum dieser Beitrag nun etwas verspätet erscheint. Unser Text sollte ohne Vorwissen verständlich sein: eine Auseinandersetzung mit der Ursprungskritik ist aber von Vorteil. Zugleich soll unser Beitrag auch eine Vertiefung in vielerlei Fragen bieten, die nicht immer direkt mit der Kritik zusammenhängt bzw. sie mancherorts nur streift.


Bereits im ersten Abschnitt liest sich ein Punkt, der so nicht stehen gelassen werden kann. In der Aufzählung zur angemessenen Militanz vom 11. Oktober letzten Jahres – wie die Autorin es selbst nennt – wird mit den durchaus nachvollziehbaren zerlegten Bankgebäuden und dem Trotz gegenüber den Polizeisperren dann auch gleich die Brandstiftung eines Restaurants in einem Atemzug genannt. Doch wer diese Flamme gelegt hat und aus welcher Überlegung heraus, ist bis heute ungeklärt – ein Agent Provocateur ist nicht auszuschliessen. Unabhängig davon, möchten wir der Autor*in dennoch widersprechen, dass diese angemessen war. Unser Widerspruch dazu soll nicht moralistisch gelesen werden: Was ist schon ein Feuer vor einem Restaurant – wo kein Mensch physisch zu Schaden kam – im Kontrast dazu, dass dieser Staat einen Völkermord unterstützt und breite Teile der Bevölkerung diesem gleichgültig bis unterstützend begegnen? Natürlich ist es geheuchelt, wenn ausgerechnet da plötzlich alle möglichen Nutzniesser*innen des Imperialismus die Frage der Gerechtigkeit aufmachen, diesen Vorfall in den Fokus nehmen und dabei nicht selten den Protest als Ganzes delegitimieren. Wenn in unseren aktuellen Verhältnissen aber zur Militanz gegriffen wird, dann sollte sowohl das Ziel der Militanz, das Ausmass und die inhaltliche Begleitung davon aus revolutionärer und klassenbewusster Perspektive heraus möglichst einleuchtend sein: das sehen wir bei diesem Feuerlegen alles als nicht gegeben an.


Anschliessend wird der Demotag diesen Jahres folgendermassen beschrieben: «Dieses Mal ohne grossen Demonstrationszug und ohne Gewalt: Kleingruppen verteilten sich in der Stadt, färbten Brunnen, malten mit Kreide und kleisterten vereinzelt Plakate.» Damit werden zentrale Facetten der Demo ausgeklammert, die dann auch im restlichen Text vergeblich gesucht werden. Um das Bild also wieder gerade zu rücken, ist folgendes festzuhalten: Die Bewegung ist in der ganzen Stadt präsent gewesen – trotz Hunderte von Bullen aus der ganzen Schweiz. Es gab verschiedene Blöcke und nicht nur "diesen einen" oder "Kleingruppen", wie es die Leitmedien – und nun auch das Lamm – darstellen und die Bewegung damit kleinreden. Eine Velodemo fuhr entschlossen vom Eigerplatz bis zum Bundesplatz durch alle möglichen Strassen und Gassen. Über 250 Menschen, die im Demoticker die Aufrufe mitverfolgten, haben sich bei der Zytglogge, auf dem Waisenhausplatz und in der gesamten unteren Altstadt die Strasse genommen. Zu guter Letzt kam dann auch der Demozug, der sich durch den Breitsch und die Lorraine bewegte, zum Banhofsplatz hoch. An all diesen Orten wurden gehaltvolle Reden gehalten – etwa zur medialen Komplizenschaft von Tamedia im Genozid, zum kurdischen Befreiungskampf oder eine Rede zu Palästina und imperialer Besatzung generell. In allen Demos wurden laut und entschlossen Parolen geschrien. Auch Aktionen wie bpsw. der Bannerdrop am Bahnhof und die Trumpfigur auf dem Bubenbergplatz oder, dass sich ca. 1'000 Leute den Bahnhofsplatz nahmen, ist der Autor*in keine Erwähnung wert. Die Autor*in bringt die Demo also um eine Menge Inhalte und Formen, zeichnet das Bild einer umkämpferischen, beinahe kindlichen Bewegung und streicht jegliche Informationen heraus, die diesem Zerrbild zuwider laufen. Zu einer ernsthaften und solidarischen Kritik würde an dieser Stelle die Erwähnung aller Akzente der Demo dazugehören – gerade, wenn diese mit dem Inhalt der …

author: Farai Shawn Matiashe
title: Electrification in Africa means closing the energy access gap and reducing energy poverty
content:
At the United Nations climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, the COP31 presidency is pushing for a global target to increase electricity’s share of final energy consumption to

35% by 2035

, a central pillar of the conference.


The COP31 Turkish presidency proposed the global electrification target at the 2026 Bonn Climate Change Conference in June to encourage countries and businesses worldwide to electrify transport, buildings, and industry using renewable energy, helping to accelerate the shift away from fossil fuels.


But as delegates gather in the Mediterranean country for the climate summit known as Conference of the Parties 31 (COP31), the target risks overlooking the different energy realities Africa faces unless they place energy access and development at its centre.


For industrialised economies, electrification is all about replacing existing fossil fuel systems, while in Africa, some countries still want to build electricity infrastructure and distribution networks.


The new target, up from the current global rate of electrification of about 20%, comes at a time when Africa faces energy poverty and a huge electricity access gap.


About 600 million people lack electricity access, with half of them living in three countries, namely Nigeria, Ethiopia and the Democratic Republic of Congo,

according

 to the International Energy Agency.


Sub-Saharan Africa accounts for roughly 85% of the global population lacking electricity.


The 35 by 35 risks widening existing energy inequality


Dr Chigozie Nweke-Eze, founder of the Integrated Africa Power (IAP), an enterprise focused on solving energy and infrastructure deficits across the African continent, said the proposed 35 by 35 target risks overlooking the different energy realities Africa faces.


Some of the solar panels which are part of a solar mini grid in Hakwata Chipinge in Zimbabwe. Photo by Farai Shawn Matiashe.


“There is a fundamental distinction between the energy transition in industrialised economies and that in many African countries,” he said.


“There is also a risk that a global target expressed as the share of electricity in final energy consumption could obscure inequalities between countries.”


Nweke-Eze said a global increase in electricity consumption does not mean improved energy access for populations that remain disconnected from the grid.


“Nor does it automatically address the affordability and reliability of electricity for households and small businesses,” he said.


In industrialised economies, electrification is largely about replacing petrol and diesel vehicles with electric vehicles, and industrial gas boilers and household gas heaters with electric heat pumps.


For Africa, it means it must build entirely new energy systems to support its expanding population and development aspirations. The continent is simultaneously attempting to shift towards renewable energy that is both cleaner and more sustainable.


Nweke-Eze said electrification cannot happen at scale without adequate generation capacity, transmission and distribution networks, reliable electricity supply, and affordable connections.


But Nweke-Eze said that Africa should be an integral part of the 35-by-35 ambition, with the target adapted to the continent’s unique energy context, recognising its diverse starting points and prioritising pathways that expand energy access and address the needs of underserved communities.


Another initiative

launched

 at COP31 is the Global Rooftop Solar Declaration, which aims to double the number of solar-powered households globally to 300 million by 2030. Endorsed by a cross-continental coalition including Kenya and Nigeria, the initiative offers a practical pathway to addressing Africa’s energy access gap by accelerating the deployment of household solar, particularly in communities underserved by centralised electricity grids.


It focuses on overcoming barriers such as high upfront costs, complex permitting processes and skills shortages that can slow the adoption of decentralised

solar solutions

.


This, Nweke-Eze argued, also requires a broader understanding of how progress towards electrification is measured. Africa should not be judged solely against the pace at which industrialised economies replace fossil-fuel technologies, but also by how effectively its countries expand electricity access, develop productive energy infrastructure and improve the quality of energy services.
